days.title: Cloud Identity: Federation, Provisioning and Super Admin Protection

concepts.heading: Provisioning and Sign-In Are Two Separate Jobs
concepts.body: A company that keeps Active Directory as its source of truth needs two flows into Cloud Identity. Provisioning creates the users and groups. Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) queries the LDAP directory and uses the Directory API to add, modify or delete users in Cloud Identity. It is usually run on-premises because Active Directory holds sensitive data and uses unencrypted LDAP by default, and GCDS talks to Cloud Identity over HTTPS. Other IdPs, such as Microsoft Entra ID, offer their own provisioning connectors that do the same job. Sign-in is the second flow: with SAML single sign-on, Google redirects the user to the IdP, which verifies the credential and applies MFA, and returns a signed assertion. The assertion's NameID must equal the user's primary email address, which is case sensitive; aliases are not considered. An IdP that sends an employee number as the NameID leaves Google nothing to match. When two forests feed one Cloud Identity account through two GCDS instances, give each instance exclusion rules for the users it does not own, or each will treat the other's users as deleted and suspend them.

concepts.heading: Protecting Super Admins
concepts.body: Single sign-on applies to everyone except super admins. When sign-on starts at Google, super admins are never redirected to the IdP and are asked for a password, so any MFA the IdP enforces never challenges them. They can still use IdP-initiated sign-in, which creates a second risk, name squatting: if a super admin such as alice-admin@example.com has no counterpart in the IdP, someone who can create IdP users can create a user with that email and sign in as the admin. Google's guidance is a set of layered controls. Enforce Google 2-step verification for all personalized super admins. Turn on post-SSO verification so a sign-in that arrives from the IdP is still challenged by Google. Keep Cloud Identity identities a subset of IdP identities, with every account created and removed by the IdP lifecycle. Use dedicated admin accounts with a naming scheme such as an -admin suffix, kept apart from daily accounts, and avoid network masks because they let users sidestep IdP MFA.

concepts.heading: User Lifecycle Automation
concepts.body: Treat the IdP or HR system as the source of truth and automate every joiner, mover and leaver event, because provisioning is one-way and manual edits in Cloud Identity are not carried back. Suspension must be mirrored. Disabling a leaver only at the IdP stops new single sign-on, yet an active browser session, OAuth tokens already issued, budget alert emails and any password sign-in path can survive. Suspending the user in Cloud Identity ends sessions, invalidates tokens and revokes the rest, and it is non-destructive: data is kept and IAM roles stay as they were. Deletion needs more care. If the IdP account is deleted but the Cloud Identity user stays, a new hire who receives the same email address maps to the old account and inherits its groups and files. Deleting at once is destructive and may break a retention rule. The documented answers are to keep the user suspended for the retention period and then delete it in both systems, or to suspend and rename the primary email to a unique obsolete-date name, then delete it after retention.

concepts.heading: Groups and Unmanaged Accounts
concepts.body: Grant IAM roles to groups, not individuals, and choose the group type that fits the source of membership. The Cloud Identity Groups API supports Google Groups, dynamic groups, security groups and locked groups. A dynamic group manages its own membership from a query on employee attributes, for example every user whose job role is Technical Writer, so access follows HR data without anyone editing lists. A security group is a Google Group used specifically to control access to organizational resources. A locked group restricts edits to core attributes and membership to authorized administrators, which keeps a group mirrored from the IdP from drifting when owners edit it by hand. Unmanaged accounts are a separate hazard. Adding a domain to Cloud Identity does not stop employees from registering consumer accounts with corporate addresses. Creating a managed user for every employee, with the corporate address as primary email or alias, blocks that sign-up, and unmanaged consumer accounts that already exist cannot use your SSO settings.

examPoints: A question where super admins sign in with passwords that the IdP's MFA never challenges points to enforcing Google 2-step verification for them plus post-SSO verification, and a question about an IdP user colliding with a Cloud Identity admin points to keeping Cloud Identity identities a subset of IdP identities.

A question about a leaver who still has working sessions, tokens or budget alert mail points to propagating suspension to Cloud Identity, and one about a reused email address and a retention period points to suspend, rename, then delete after retention.

A question about two forests and two GCDS instances points to exclusion rules per instance, one about membership that follows a job attribute points to a dynamic group, and one about drift from the IdP points to a locked group.

quiz.q: HR deletes a departed employee's IdP account. The Cloud Identity user is never touched, and months later a new hire receives the same email address and inherits the former employee's files and group memberships. Compliance requires keeping the leaver's data for 90 days. What should the lifecycle automation do when the IdP account is deleted?
choices: Delete the Cloud Identity user immediately so that its data is removed together with the IdP account, and rely on backups for retention
Leave the Cloud Identity user active and block the account only at the IdP, which already prevents any single sign-on
Move the user to a separate organizational unit and keep the original email address so that audits can still find it
Suspend the user, rename its primary email to a unique obsolete name, and delete it after the retention period
quiz.explain: Suspension keeps the data for the 90 days, and the unique name means a future hire can never map to the old account. Deleting at once is tempting but destroys data the retention rule needs, and leaving the account in place keeps the name-reuse and inherited-access risk.

quiz.q: A company uses SAML single sign-on, and its IdP enforces MFA for every employee. A review shows that three super admins still sign in with Google passwords and are never challenged for a second factor. Which change addresses the gap?
choices: Add a network mask to the single sign-on settings so that office sign-ins are sent to the IdP for the MFA challenge
Enforce Google 2-step verification for super admins and turn on post-SSO verification for IdP-initiated sign-in
Ask the IdP team to extend its MFA policy to the super admins, since the IdP already controls every other account
Remove the super admins from the IdP so that only Google passwords remain and one set of credentials is checked
quiz.explain: Super admins are not redirected to the IdP, so Google itself must challenge them. A network mask is tempting but Google advises against it because users can change location to avoid the IdP, and extending the IdP policy cannot reach a sign-in that never goes there.

days.recap: Provision with GCDS or an IdP adapter, sign in with SAML where the NameID is the primary email, protect super admins with Google 2-step and post-SSO verification, mirror suspensions and deletions from the IdP, and use dynamic or locked groups so membership follows the source.

days.title: Service Accounts: Default Accounts, Keys and Short-Lived Credentials

concepts.heading: Default and Dedicated Service Accounts
concepts.body: Default service accounts are created automatically when you use services such as Compute Engine or App Engine, and you are responsible for managing them afterwards. Depending on organization policy, such an account may be granted the Editor role on the project automatically. Enforce the iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts constraint to stop the automatic grant; organizations created on or after May 3, 2024 have it enforced by default. That constraint does not stop a rushed engineer from granting Editor by hand, which the iam.managed.preventPrivilegedBasicRolesForDefaultServiceAccounts managed constraint does, for automatic and manual grants alike. Prefer single-purpose service accounts: Cloud Audit Logs name the service account but not the application using it, so applications that share one cannot be told apart, and roles accumulate over time. Granting Service Account User lets a principal attach a service account to a resource, and that principal can then reach whatever the account can reach, so grant it on the one runtime account a pipeline needs rather than on the whole project.

concepts.heading: Service Account Keys: Avoid, Constrain, Respond
concepts.body: A key is a long-lived credential that grants access wherever it is copied, so Google's guidance is to avoid keys when another method exists. When you cannot, constrain them. The iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint blocks new external keys and Cloud Storage HMAC keys, and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload blocks uploaded public keys. Do not leave the Editor role in projects that allow key creation or upload: Editor can mint a key for a more privileged account in the project, which is a privilege escalation path. The iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours constraint sets a lifetime for newly created keys only, so older keys need their own clean-up, and Google advises against expiry for production workloads because an expired key causes an outage; use rotation there. Do not store keys in Secret Manager. For leaks, set Service Account Key Exposure Response to DISABLE_KEY and Google disables keys it finds exposed. A disabled exposed key can be re-enabled to end an outage, but treat it as compromised, move the workload to a keyless identity and delete the key.

concepts.heading: Auditing Usage and Retiring Accounts
concepts.body: Cleaning up service accounts starts with evidence of use. Service account insights identify accounts that have not been used in the past 90 days, and the Key Authentication Events metric shows when a key was last used and how often. Both are tracked per project. Activity Analyzer in Policy Intelligence shows when service accounts and keys last called a Google API. Retire in two steps: disable first, watch for breakage, delete later. Disabling is reversible and exposes dependants quickly, whereas deleting and then recreating an account with the same name does not restore its role bindings. Audit logs matter just as much. With a key, the logs show only the service account, so a shared key hides which application or machine acted. When keys are unavoidable, give each application its own account and each machine its own key so the key name in the log narrows down the source. Lateral movement insights flag roles that let an account in one project impersonate an account in another.

concepts.heading: Short-Lived Credentials and Central Control
concepts.body: The most secure way to authenticate as a service account is a short-lived OAuth 2.0 access token, which expires after one hour by default. Most of the time you never request it yourself: an account attached to a Compute Engine VM supplies tokens through Application Default Credentials, the gcloud --impersonate-service-account flag creates them, and Workload Identity Federation exchanges outside credentials for them. The Service Account Credentials API can also create ID tokens, self-signed JWTs and signed blobs. For central control, the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountCreation constraint stops teams creating accounts in application projects, and cross-project attachment lets workloads there run as accounts created in one controlled identity project. Adding iam.restrictCrossProjectServiceAccountLienRemoval means only principals with the lien permission on the organization can remove the lien that protects that identity project. A question that bans keys but still needs a workload to authenticate usually has one of these keyless answers.

examPoints: A question about Editor still appearing on default service accounts after the automatic-grant constraint points to the managed constraint that blocks Editor and Owner for default service accounts, whether granted automatically or manually.

A question where nobody should create keys points to the key creation and upload constraints, not key expiry, and a question about a key found in a public repository points to Key Exposure Response set to DISABLE_KEY, then moving off the key.

A question about unused accounts points to service account insights and disable-before-delete, and one about tracing activity to an application points to one service account per application and one key per machine.

quiz.q: An organization enforced the legacy constraint that stops automatic Editor grants to default service accounts. Auditors still find the Compute Engine default service account holding Editor in new projects, because engineers granted it manually to fix failing deployments. Which control closes this gap?
choices: Enforce the managed constraint that denies Editor and Owner to default service accounts however they are granted
Set the key expiry constraint so that any credential held by the default account is unusable after a short period
Grant Service Account User on the default account to a small group so that only that group can attach it to resources
Delete the default service accounts in each new project and let teams create their own after each project is made
quiz.explain: The managed constraint refuses the Editor and Owner grant however it is attempted. The legacy constraint only stops the automatic grant, and key expiry or Service Account User changes do not remove a role that has already been bound.

quiz.q: A security team sets the key expiry constraint so that new service account keys last seven days. Which statement about this control is correct?
choices: It also invalidates existing keys after seven days, so older keys need no separate clean-up once the policy is set
It prevents anyone from creating keys, because a key with a short lifetime is treated as a violation of the policy
It applies to newly created keys only, so existing keys remain valid and need their own review and removal
It is the recommended protection for production workloads, since rotation then happens automatically every week
quiz.explain: Expiry limits keys created after the policy is enforced. Preventing creation is a different constraint, and Google advises against expiry for production because an expired key causes an outage; rotation is the production answer.

days.recap: Block privileged grants to default accounts, give each application its own account, prefer attached identities and short-lived tokens over keys, constrain and expire the keys you cannot avoid, auto-disable leaked keys, and retire accounts by disabling before deleting.

days.title: Federation and Impersonation: Workforce, Workload and Service Accounts

concepts.heading: Workforce Identity Federation for People
concepts.body: Workforce Identity Federation lets employees, partners and contractors sign in to Google Cloud with accounts that stay in your OIDC or SAML 2.0 IdP. It is sync-less, so no Google identities are created and GCDS is not needed. A workforce identity pool is configured at the organization level, and each provider exchanges the IdP credential through the Security Token Service for a short-lived Google Cloud access token. Attribute mapping is where designs go wrong. google.subject is required and appears in audit logs; do not map a mutable value such as an email address, because if the IdP changes it the user loses all access granted to the old value. google.groups is optional, and a user who belongs to more than 400 mapped groups cannot sign in, so map only the groups your IAM policies use. Attribute conditions are evaluated on every token. If the IdP is a public service that uses one issuer for all customers, a condition pinning your tenant is what stops another customer's validly signed token from being accepted. Audit logs record access with the pool ID.

concepts.heading: Workload Identity Federation for Software
concepts.body: Workload Identity Federation gives workloads outside Google Cloud access without a service account key. It supports AWS, Azure, GitHub and GitLab, on-premises Active Directory, X.509 client certificates and any OIDC or SAML 2.0 IdP. The workload presents its credential to the Security Token Service, which returns a federated token. A provider defines the mapping from the IdP credential: for AWS the default maps google.subject to the caller ARN and attribute.aws_role to the assumed role. An attribute condition is a CEL expression that rejects credentials that fail it, which restricts who may use the pool and avoids the confused deputy problem when one IdP serves many clouds. Where an issuer such as a self-hosted GitHub Enterprise has no public discovery endpoint, upload its JWKS to the pool instead of exposing a URL. Organization policy backs the design: the iam.workloadIdentityPoolAwsAccounts and iam.workloadIdentityPoolProviders constraints limit which AWS accounts and identity providers any project may trust, even for project owners.

concepts.heading: Granting Access to Federated Principals
concepts.body: Federated workloads can be granted access in two ways. Direct resource access grants IAM roles to the federated principal itself, and Google recommends it where the API supports it. Service account impersonation grants the principal the Workload Identity User role on a service account, and the workload then gets the account's short-lived tokens, which is the fallback for APIs that do not accept federated principals. Principals are written as principal:// for one subject or principalSet:// for everything sharing an attribute or group. Scope matters. A GitHub pipeline design uses a provider condition on the organization and a principalSet on the repository attribute, so only one repository can use the production service account. For an autoscaled AWS fleet, a per-instance subject binding breaks when instances are replaced, whereas a principalSet on the role attribute keeps working because every replacement runs under the same role. Workforce identities are authorized the same way, with principal identifiers for the pool, subject or groups.

concepts.heading: Service Account Impersonation
concepts.body: Impersonation lets a principal act as a service account without holding a key. It needs the iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken permission, which is in the Service Account Token Creator role, and it yields short-lived credentials. Service Account User is different: it lets a principal attach the account to a resource but does not allow creating credentials or using the gcloud impersonation flag. The main security gain is accountability. When a principal impersonates an account, most audit logs show both the impersonated service account and the identity that created the credentials, while a key records only the service account. A Terraform pipeline that runs as tf-prod with a downloaded key leaves nobody to blame for an unapproved change; the same pipeline impersonating tf-prod leaves a caller on every request. The Google Cloud console always uses your own credentials, so you cannot impersonate there. For Cloud Storage only, a Credential Access Boundary downscopes a short-lived token to a single bucket, which is the efficient way to give each customer a credential limited to its own data.

examPoints: A question about contractors signing in through a SaaS IdP with a shared issuer points to an attribute condition that pins the tenant, and a question where access vanished after the IdP changed email addresses points to mapping google.subject to an immutable identifier.

A question about GitHub or GitLab pipelines deploying without keys points to Workload Identity Federation with a provider attribute condition and a principalSet binding to the repository, and one about a private issuer with no public endpoint points to uploading the JWKS.

A question about attributing a change to a person or pipeline run points to impersonation with the Token Creator role instead of a shared key, and one about per-customer bucket access from a broad account points to a Credential Access Boundary.

quiz.q: A workforce identity pool maps google.subject to each user's email address. During a rebrand, the IdP team moves every mailbox to a new domain. Everyone can still sign in, but all access granted to the old addresses is gone. What is the lasting fix?
choices: Map google.subject to an immutable IdP identifier and grant access again to the principals built from it
Raise the group limit in the pool so that each user belongs to more groups and recovers the lost access
Switch the provider from authorization code flow to implicit flow so that fresh claims arrive with every sign-in
Add the old domain to the attribute condition so that tokens from the previous addresses are accepted again
quiz.explain: Bindings match the literal subject value, so a changed email is a different principal. An immutable identifier prevents a repeat. The attribute condition decides whether a token is accepted, not which principal it becomes, so it cannot restore the old grants.

quiz.q: A company deploys from GitHub Actions to Google Cloud. Any workflow in its GitHub organization may deploy to development, but only the payments-infra repository may deploy to production, and all workflows share one provider. Which design enforces this?
choices: Create a service account key for production and store it as a secret that only the payments-infra repository can read
Grant the production service account to the whole pool so that any workflow in the organization can impersonate it
Create one pool per environment and rely on branch names in each workflow file to separate development and production
Add a provider condition on the organization and bind a principalSet for that repository to the production account
quiz.explain: The condition keeps other organizations out and the repository-scoped principalSet means no other repository can impersonate the production account. A stored key brings back a long-lived secret, and granting the whole pool gives every workflow production access.

days.recap: Use Workforce Identity Federation for people and Workload Identity Federation for software, map immutable subjects and pin tenants with attribute conditions, prefer direct access with principalSet bindings, and impersonate service accounts so logs show who acted.

days.title: Authentication: SAML, OAuth, Token Types and Two-Step Verification

concepts.heading: Where Authentication Happens in a Federated Design
concepts.body: In a federated Cloud Identity account, Google is the service provider and the IdP is the authority. A user enters a primary email address, is redirected to the IdP, authenticates there, and returns with a signed SAML assertion that Google verifies. Password rules and MFA therefore belong to the IdP, because provisioning carries identities, not credentials. SSO is an account-level setting that applies to every user except super admins, which matters for a holding company where one subsidiary needs a corporate IdP and another wants Google-managed passwords: a single account cannot mix those models without scoping or a second account. A user with no matching IdP identity fails to sign in, so provision and allow SSO only for the people who need Google services. Then a lax access rule can reach only that small population, a useful second barrier. Keep the same identity across the Google and IdP sign-on screens to avoid confusing users. Details of password and session rules are product settings; for the exam, know which system owns them.

concepts.heading: Sessions and Second Factors
concepts.body: Once a SAML sign-in succeeds, Google creates a session that is valid across Google services. You can control the Google Cloud session length, which covers the console, the gcloud CLI and other API clients. A short Google session only forces a real login if the IdP session is shorter: when the IdP session outlasts the Google one, re-authentication is silent and the shortening achieves nothing. Plan the two lengths together. For second factors, regular SSO users get theirs from the IdP. If the IdP cannot do MFA, post-SSO verification makes Google perform an additional check after the user returns. Super admins are the exception because they are not redirected: enforce Google 2-step verification for them, which can be applied account-wide, by organizational unit or by group, and prefer account-wide so nobody is missed. Machine super admins that cannot use 2-step verification should be few, and a dedicated enforcement group covers the rest. Avoid network masks, which let users choose when the IdP is bypassed.

concepts.heading: Token Types
concepts.body: Google Cloud groups tokens in three categories. Access tokens let clients call APIs. Token-granting tokens, such as refresh tokens and authorization codes, let clients obtain other tokens later. Identity tokens let a client learn who the user is. Most are bearer tokens, usable by anyone holding them, whereas bound tokens need proof of the rightful client and so resist theft. A user access token is restricted to OAuth scopes, which is why a developer with Storage Admin can still be denied by a token that lacks the right scope: a call needs both a suitable scope and an IAM permission. A user ID token is a JWT signed by Google that authenticates the user, valid for one hour and not revocable. A web backend that only needs to know who signed in should verify that token, which carries no right to call Google APIs. A refresh token is tied to a client and can be revoked; a federated refresh token, issued for a workforce identity pool principal, cannot be revoked and lasts as long as the workforce session.

concepts.heading: OAuth, Service Accounts and Delegation
concepts.body: OAuth 2.0 lets an application act for a user after consent, while a service account lets an application act as itself, authorized through IAM. Prefer one of these. Workspace APIs such as the Directory API sit outside IAM roles, which tempts teams to use domain-wide delegation, where a service account acts on behalf of any user in the domain. Google advises it only when the OAuth approach is not practical. A delegation token authenticates a user and authorizes the service account to act as that user; it expires after one hour and cannot be revoked. If you must use delegation, create a dedicated user for each delegating service account in the IdP and provision it, so Cloud Identity stays a subset of the IdP, and avoid service account keys for the signing step. Because delegation lets a Google Workspace super admin impersonate any user in the account, Google also recommends keeping Google Workspace and Google Cloud administration responsibilities separate to reduce the number of super admins.

examPoints: A question where a SAML sign-in is rejected although the user authenticated at the IdP points to the NameID not matching the user's primary email address, and one about who enforces MFA after SSO points to the IdP, with post-SSO verification as the Google-side fallback.
A question where a shortened Google session never prompts for credentials points to an IdP session that is longer than the Google session, so the IdP session must be shorter.

A question about telling a backend who the user is points to the user ID token, and one about cutting off a stolen laptop's access points to revoking refresh tokens, noting that federated refresh tokens last until the workforce session ends.

quiz.q: An internal tool uses OAuth. A security engineer wants to know how quickly a stolen laptop's tokens can be cut off. Employees sign in as Cloud Identity users, and contractors come through a workforce identity pool. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Both kinds of refresh token can be revoked at once, so the account can be locked and every token dies immediately
A refresh token can be revoked, but a federated refresh token cannot and lasts until its workforce session ends
Neither kind of refresh token can be revoked, so only waiting for expiry ends access to every Google service
A federated refresh token can be revoked, but a Cloud Identity refresh token lasts as long as the account exists
quiz.explain: Refresh tokens are tied to a client and revocable. Federated refresh tokens are linked to the workforce identity session and remain valid until it expires, so contractors need a short workforce session.

quiz.q: After enabling SAML single sign-on, a company shortens the Google session length to 8 hours. Employees say they almost never see a login prompt after expiry, and the IdP keeps its own sessions for 30 days. How can security make the shorter session meaningful?
choices: Shorten the IdP session below the Google session so that an expired Google session leads to a real login
Lengthen the Google session beyond the IdP session so that fewer redirects reach the IdP and its prompts
Add a network mask for the office range so that employees there are always asked for a password at Google
Turn off single sign-on for ordinary users so that every expiry produces a Google password prompt instead
quiz.explain: When Google redirects an expired session to an IdP session that is still alive, re-authentication is silent. Making the IdP session shorter forces credentials and MFA again; a network mask is advised against because it lets users sidestep IdP MFA.

days.recap: The IdP owns passwords and MFA in a federated design, super admins need Google 2-step verification, the IdP session must be shorter than the Google session, and know access, refresh, federated refresh and ID tokens by what each can do and whether it can be revoked.

days.title: Authorization I: Roles, Conditions, Deny Policies and Privileged Access Manager

concepts.heading: Roles, Scope and Separation of Duties
concepts.body: Least privilege starts with the role choice. Basic roles contain thousands of permissions and should be avoided in production, so grant the most limited predefined role, or a custom role, and use role recommendations to replace a basic role. Grant roles to groups rather than individual users, which keeps policies short and makes offboarding a membership change. Separation of duties is built from role design: Project IAM Admin and Folder IAM Admin let a team modify allow policies without direct read, write or administrative access to every resource, while Owner allows nearly everything including policy changes and should be reserved for nearly universal need. Scope is the other lever. Allow policies are inherited down the hierarchy and the effective policy is the union of what is set at the resource and above, so a role granted high in the tree reaches everything below it. Cloud Storage adds a second system, ACLs. Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs, so only IAM grants access to the bucket and its objects, which gives one place to audit.

concepts.heading: IAM Conditions
concepts.body: IAM Conditions are CEL expressions that make a grant, a denial or a boundary depend on context. They work in allow policy role bindings, including those managed by Privileged Access Manager, in deny rules, and in Principal Access Boundary policy bindings. In allow bindings you can test the resource type, the resource name and the request time, so contractors can hold a role only on weekdays or only until a date. resource.name matching uses startsWith() or endsWith() rather than wildcard patterns. Not every resource type accepts conditions on its own policy, but you can grant the role on the project or organization and add a condition on type or name. A support group that may restart only instances whose names start with stg- is solved this way, and it covers instances created later. Tags let access follow metadata: one conditional binding on a folder for resources tagged env=dev means that re-tagging a resource changes who has access with no policy edit. Google advises against more than 100 conditional bindings in one allow policy.

concepts.heading: Deny Policies
concepts.body: A deny policy states what principals can never do, whatever roles they hold. IAM checks deny policies before allow policies, and they are attached to an organization, folder or project and inherited by everything below, so a lower level cannot loosen a higher deny. A rule lists denied principals, optional exception principals, the denied permissions and an optional condition. Exceptions let you carve out an administrators group from a broad denial. Permission groups use a wildcard to deny, for example, every permission for one resource type and include permissions added in future, so the guardrail stays complete. A classic design is one organization-level rule that stops everyone except project-admins from deleting projects tagged env=prod, instead of editing every role grant. Know the limits. Denial conditions recognize only resource tag functions, so a time-of-day restriction belongs in a conditional allow binding, not a deny rule. If a denial condition cannot be evaluated, the rule applies, so deny fails closed. Rehearse a new rule with Policy Simulator before enforcing it.

concepts.heading: Privileged Access Manager
concepts.body: Privileged Access Manager (PAM) replaces standing admin rights with just-in-time elevation. An entitlement defines the roles to grant, who may request them, whether a justification is required, the maximum duration, and optionally who must approve. A requester receives the roles until the duration ends, then PAM removes them, and audit logs show who had access to what and when. Match the entitlement to the need. Emergency access for responders at night needs no approval but requires a justification and a short duration. Sensitive production access can require approval and a business justification, and multi-level, multi-party approvals can enforce separation of duties, with service accounts as approvers to automate ticket validation. PAM supports predefined roles, custom roles and the Admin, Writer and Reader basic roles, but not Owner, Editor or Viewer. It works by adding and removing time-based conditional bindings in allow policies, so do not edit those bindings manually, and if Terraform manages the policy use non-authoritative resources so it does not overwrite them. PAM adds workflow and audit that a conditional expiry alone lacks.

examPoints: A question about stopping everyone except one group from deleting projects tagged prod points to an organization-level deny policy with a tag condition and exception principals, and one about blocking access outside business hours points to a conditional allow binding, since denial conditions know only tags.

A question about restarting only instances named stg- in a shared project points to a narrow role on the project with a resource name condition, and one about access that follows a resource's tag points to a tag condition on a folder-level binding.

A question about no standing admin rights points to Privileged Access Manager, with no approval but a justification for emergency access, and with multi-party approvals when separation of duties is required.

quiz.q: A platform team grants broad roles to developers but must stop anyone outside the project-admins group from deleting projects tagged env=prod, without editing every role grant. Which control fits best?
choices: An organization-level deny policy on project deletion with a tag condition and the admins group as an exception
A conditional allow binding on every developer group that lists the project deletion permission and the prod tag
A custom role with the project deletion permission removed, granted to developers in each production project
A Principal Access Boundary policy that limits developers to resources in projects that carry the dev tag only
quiz.explain: One deny rule is inherited by every project under it, targets prod-tagged projects through its tag condition, and the exception principals exempt the admin group. Conditional allow bindings add access and cannot remove access granted by other roles.

quiz.q: Contractors hold Compute Instance Admin on a project. The company wants to block those permissions outside business hours and on weekends. A colleague proposes a deny policy whose denial condition tests the request time. Why does that fail, and what is the right way?
choices: Deny policies cannot apply to groups, so each contractor needs an individual rule that names the working hours
The time test works in a deny rule, but only at the organization level, so the rule must be attached there
Denial conditions know only resource tags, so the schedule belongs in a conditional allow binding
Time conditions are valid only in Principal Access Boundary bindings, so a boundary policy should hold the schedule
quiz.explain: Time attributes are available in allow policy conditions, while denial conditions recognize only resource tag functions. Deny rules do accept groups, and Principal Access Boundary bindings are not the place for working-hours logic.

days.recap: Grant narrow roles to groups at the smallest useful scope, use conditions for context, deny policies for central guardrails that always win, and Privileged Access Manager for justified, approved, time-limited elevation.

days.title: Authorization II and Hierarchy: Context, Policy Intelligence, Boundaries and Organization Policy

concepts.heading: Access Context Manager Defines, Others Enforce
concepts.body: Access Context Manager lets an organization define attribute-based access control through an access policy, an organization-wide container for access levels and service perimeters. Access levels describe what a request must look like to be honored, such as device type and operating system, IP address or user identity. Service perimeters define sandboxes of resources that can exchange data internally but cannot export it. Access Context Manager does not itself block a request: it holds the definitions, and enforcement happens in the products that consult them, such as VPC Service Controls and Identity-Aware Proxy, which Google lists as Chrome Enterprise Premium components. So an internal admin app behind Identity-Aware Proxy that must be reachable by the admin group only from managed corporate devices is built by defining an access level for managed devices and attaching it to the group's IAP role binding as a condition. Defining the requirement once in Access Context Manager keeps it consistent wherever a product enforces it.

concepts.heading: Policy Intelligence
concepts.body: Policy Intelligence tools answer different questions, and the exam tests which one fits. Policy Analyzer answers who has access to what, for IAM allow policies and for organization policies. Policy Troubleshooter answers why, for example why a user holds a permission or cannot view a bucket's policy; a VPC Service Controls troubleshooter exists too. Policy Simulator answers what would change: it exists for allow, deny and Principal Access Boundary policies, and for organization policies that enforce custom constraints, and each simulator evaluates only one policy type, ignoring the others. Use it before tightening a role or enforcing a deny rule. The IAM recommender produces role recommendations from permission usage, but it considers only IAM, so access control lists and Kubernetes RBAC must be reviewed separately, it makes no recommendations for conditional role bindings, and it needs an observation period of 90 days by default. It never applies changes by itself. Activity Analyzer, service account insights and lateral movement insights cover service accounts, which Day 2 described.

concepts.heading: Principal Access Boundary
concepts.body: Allow and deny policies attach to resources. A Principal Access Boundary (PAB) policy attaches to a set of principals and defines the resources they are eligible to access. By default every principal is eligible for any resource. Once a principal is bound to PAB policies, it is eligible only for the union of the resources they list, so an employee or service account could be limited to your organization and could not use a role granted by another organization, which counters phishing and data exfiltration. A principal bound to none stays eligible for everything, so removing the last policy widens access. Binding goes to principal sets such as all identities in a workforce identity pool or a workload identity pool, and each set can have up to 10 PAB policies. The policy blocks only permissions covered by its enforcement version. If a cross-boundary action still works, the permission may not be in that version, and a newer version must be selected. Using latest is not recommended because access can disappear unexpectedly. Preview the effect with Policy Simulator for PAB.

concepts.heading: Folders, Projects and Organization Policy at Scale
concepts.body: At scale, shape the hierarchy to your organization and set controls high enough to cover many projects. The project is the trust boundary, folders group projects so a grant or deny at a folder reaches all children, and allow policies combine as a union. Organization Policy is the preventive layer: constraints that restrict what can be configured, inherited by descendants by default. A child can set its own policy; with inheritFromParent true it is merged with the parent. For list constraints deny values always win, so a deny at the folder cannot be undone by a project allowing the same value. Boolean constraints do not merge: the policy on the resource itself decides, so a folder that enforces a constraint can be overridden by a project that sets enforced to false. With inheritFromParent false the parent policy is ignored, and RestoreDefault returns the constraint's default behavior. Some constraints restrict operations by default even where nothing was set. Because a lower-level policy can reset boolean values, tightly control who holds the Organization Policy Administrator role.

examPoints: A question about requiring managed devices for an IAP-protected app points to an Access Context Manager access level used in a conditional role binding, and a reminder that Access Context Manager only defines and VPC Service Controls, IAP and IAM Conditions enforce.

A question about who has access, why a user has it, or what a change would break points to Policy Analyzer, Policy Troubleshooter and Policy Simulator, and one about a recommender suggestion with ACLs in play points to a manual review because the recommender sees only IAM.

A question where a Principal Access Boundary still lets one cross-organization action succeed points to the policy's enforcement version, and one where a project escapes an enforced boolean constraint points to a lower-level policy that replaced the inherited value.

quiz.q: A Principal Access Boundary policy limits the company's service accounts to the company's own organization. A red-team test shows that one particular action on a resource in another organization still succeeds, although most cross-organization actions are blocked. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Principal Access Boundary policies are merged with deny policies, and a missing deny rule leaves that action open
The permission is outside the policy's enforcement version, so it cannot be blocked until a newer version is set
The service account was granted the role through a group, and boundary policies only apply to individual principals
The boundary applies only to the first action in a session, so later actions on foreign resources are not evaluated
quiz.explain: A PAB policy blocks only permissions its enforcement version covers; other permissions stay usable on any resource. Boundaries do apply to principal sets and are not tied to deny rules or to sessions.

quiz.q: An organization policy with a boolean constraint is enforced at a folder. An engineer finds that one project under that folder is not restricted, and its owner set enforced to false in the project's own policy. What is the effective result on that project?
choices: The folder's value wins, because a parent's enforced setting always overrides a child's setting for boolean constraints
The two values are merged, so the constraint is partly enforced and only the stricter settings are applied
The project's own value replaces the inherited one, so the constraint is not enforced for that project
The constraint reverts to its default behavior for the whole folder until the project value is removed
quiz.explain: Boolean constraints do not merge or reconcile: the policy set on the resource decides. That is why the Organization Policy Administrator role should be tightly held, unlike list constraints where a deny always wins.

days.recap: Access Context Manager defines access levels that IAP, VPC Service Controls and conditions enforce; use Analyzer, Troubleshooter, Simulator and recommender for different questions; bound principals with PAB; and remember that boolean organization policies are replaced, not merged, below.

days.title: Perimeter I: Cloud NGFW, Cloud Armor, IAP, Load Balancer TLS and Certificate Authority Service

concepts.heading: Cloud NGFW: Policies, Rules and Tiers
concepts.body: Cloud NGFW is a distributed, stateful firewall that applies rules to VM network interfaces and to supported load balancers. Rules live in policies: hierarchical policies attach to the organization or a folder, and global or regional network policies attach to a VPC network. A rule's action decides what happens next. Allow and deny stop evaluation, so an organization-level deny cannot be overridden below, while goto_next hands the decision to the next step, which lets a project team decide. A company that must block Telnet everywhere but leave SSH to each project writes a deny for tcp:23 and a goto_next for tcp:22 at the top. Rules can target secure tags or service accounts instead of IP ranges, which gives micro-segmentation that follows the workload. Features come in three tiers. Essentials matches IP ranges, ports and protocols. Standard adds FQDN objects and threat intelligence. Enterprise adds Layer 7 security: intrusion prevention, URL filtering and TLS inspection. For internal Application Load Balancers and internal proxy Network Load Balancers, network firewall policies provide Layer 3 and Layer 4 filtering.

concepts.heading: Layer 7 Inspection and TLS Inspection
concepts.body: Intrusion prevention and URL filtering run on firewall endpoints, Google-managed zonal resources that inspect intercepted traffic. A firewall policy rule with the apply_security_profile_group action sends matching packets to the endpoint, and the threat-prevention security profile in the group defines which signatures are scanned and what happens on a match. An endpoint inspects traffic in its own zone, so workloads in two zones need an endpoint in each. URL filtering matches the host header for plain HTTP, only the plaintext SNI for HTTPS without TLS inspection, and the host header together with the SNI once TLS inspection decrypts the traffic. TLS inspection decrypts, inspects and re-encrypts toward the destination, using short-lived certificates issued through Certificate Authority Service. It needs a CA pool and a TLS inspection policy, and both are regional, so a deployment in two regions needs two of each. Clients must trust the root of that CA or they see certificate errors. The trade-off is plain: decryption shows the rules more, and in return you must distribute a root certificate to every client.

concepts.heading: Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy at the Front Door
concepts.body: Cloud Armor security policies filter requests at the edge of Google's network for external Application Load Balancers and other supported endpoints. A backend security policy covers requests that reach the backend service. An edge security policy sits upstream of the Cloud CDN cache and supports fewer parameters, so it can deny an abusive range even for objects that would be served from cache. Start new preconfigured WAF rules, which are compiled from OWASP signatures, in preview mode: matches are logged but not enforced, so false positives can be tuned first. Rate-based ban rules count requests per key such as XFF_IP and ban abusers for a set period. Adaptive Protection detects Layer 7 anomalies, but full alerts with a signature and suggested rule need Cloud Armor Enterprise. Identity-Aware Proxy adds identity: it authenticates the caller and checks IAM for the IAP-secured Web App User role, best granted to a group so joiners and leavers need no IAM edits. If backends are reachable directly, callers bypass IAP, so firewall rules should admit only the load balancer and health check ranges. Scripts send an OIDC ID token for a service account.

concepts.heading: TLS Policy, Certificates and Private CAs
concepts.body: An SSL policy sets the minimum TLS version and cipher profile for connections between clients and the load balancer, not toward the backends. Without a policy the load balancer behaves as COMPATIBLE with a minimum of TLS 1.0, so a requirement of TLS 1.2 needs one. The RESTRICTED profile narrows the cipher set. A SaaS company that terminates HTTPS for thousands of customer domains and renews certificates often uses Certificate Manager: Google-managed or self-managed certificates, selected by host name through a certificate map on the target proxy. For private PKI, Certificate Authority Service creates root and subordinate CAs. The tier belongs to the CA pool. DevOps suits high-volume, short-lived certificates that need no revocation. Enterprise supports revocation and certificate storage and is recommended for pools that issue to other CAs, so mTLS between microservices with revocable certificates belongs there. A company that keeps its root CA offline on premises can create subordinate CAs in CA Service that chain to that root, so trust stays anchored offline while the cloud CAs issue day to day.

examPoints: A question that blocks a range even for objects served from Cloud CDN points to a Cloud Armor edge security policy, and one that wants to see false positives before blocking points to a new rule in preview mode.

A question where a deny must hold at the top while a lower level still decides another port points to a hierarchical firewall policy with deny and goto_next, and one asking for threat signatures or URL filtering points to the Cloud NGFW Enterprise tier with firewall endpoints per zone.

A question about revocable certificates, subordinate CAs or an offline root points to Certificate Authority Service Enterprise pools, and one about thousands of customer domains points to Certificate Manager with a certificate map.

quiz.q: A video site serves segments through a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN. A Cloud Armor backend policy with WAF rules exists, yet one abusive address range keeps pulling cached segments. What blocks it?
choices: A higher priority deny rule for that range in the existing backend security policy, which sees every cached request
Adaptive Protection on the existing backend policy, which blocks the range automatically once it detects the traffic
A Cloud Armor edge security policy with a deny rule for that range, attached to the backend service
An Identity-Aware Proxy access list on the backend service, which stops callers outside the approved identity group
quiz.explain: The edge policy is enforced upstream of the Cloud CDN cache, so it can deny the range even for objects that would be served from cache. The backend policy is enforced only for requests that reach the backend, so cache hits never meet its rules. Adaptive Protection alerts and suggests a rule but blocks nothing by itself, and IAP checks identity, not an address range.

quiz.q: A security team must stop Telnet to every VM at the organization level, while each project team stays free to decide about SSH with its own rules. Which hierarchical firewall policy rules do this?
choices: A deny rule for tcp:23 and a goto_next rule for tcp:22, so project-level rules decide on SSH
An allow rule for tcp:22 and a deny rule for tcp:23, so every project inherits one fixed answer
A goto_next rule for tcp:23 and a deny rule for tcp:22, so project teams choose about Telnet
A deny rule for tcp:23 and a deny rule for tcp:22, so no project below can open either port
quiz.explain: A deny at the top cannot be overridden below, and goto_next passes the decision to the next step in the order, where project rules sit, so they decide on SSH. An allow at the top ends evaluation and takes the decision away from the projects. Swapping the actions delegates the wrong port. Denying both ports removes the SSH decision from the project teams.

days.recap: At the perimeter, pick the layer for the threat: Cloud NGFW for VPC traffic (Enterprise for Layer 7), Cloud Armor and IAP at the load balancer front door, an SSL policy and Certificate Manager for TLS, and Certificate Authority Service for private PKI.

days.title: Perimeter II: Public versus Private IP, Secure Web Proxy, Cloud DNS Security and API Restrictions

concepts.heading: Public versus Private IP Addresses
concepts.body: A Compute Engine VM is reachable from the internet only when it has an external address and a firewall rule admits the traffic. A security engineer removes the two conditions with separate controls, so one mistake does not expose a workload. Organization policy removes the address: the Restrict External IPs For VM instances constraint, constraints/compute.managed.vmExternalIpAccess, denies creating or updating VMs with IPv4 external addresses. Specific instances can be exempted by tagging them and scoping the enforcement with conditions on the tag; the older list constraint, constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess, instead lists the allowed instances. Firewall policy removes the second condition, and the implied deny ingress rule already blocks unsolicited inbound traffic. The managed constraint covers IPv4 only. A dual-stack subnet with an external IPv6 access type still gives a VM a publicly routable IPv6 address, so private workloads belong in subnets with internal IPv6 access, backed by ingress deny rules. Administrators then reach private VMs through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding, which needs the IAP-secured Tunnel User role, and outbound access comes from Private Google Access, Cloud NAT or Secure Web Proxy instead of a public address on every machine.

concepts.heading: Secure Web Proxy for Outbound Web Traffic
concepts.body: Secure Web Proxy is a managed outbound proxy for HTTP and HTTPS. In explicit proxy mode clients are configured to use it (next hop mode routes traffic to it instead), and it denies all outbound traffic until a rule allows it, so a missing rule fails safely. Policies are separate from the proxy, so one URL list or set of gateway security rules can be reused across proxies, and rules can match sources such as IP addresses, service accounts or secure tags. Without decryption an HTTPS request exposes only the host name. A bank that must allow www.example.com/documentation but block www.example.com/uploads therefore needs TLS inspection: the proxy presents certificates issued from a private CA pool in Certificate Authority Service, and clients must trust that root, which suits managed devices. Clients that pin certificates, such as operating system updaters, reject the proxy's certificate, so the session matcher excludes their destinations from decryption instead of switching inspection off for everyone. With Shared VPC the proxy is deployed in the host project, and it supports IPv4 only. Allowed traffic typically leaves through Cloud NAT, and activity is logged for audit.

concepts.heading: Cloud DNS Security
concepts.body: Cloud DNS has three security tools. DNSSEC signs a public zone so resolvers can detect forged or poisoned answers. It authenticates answers and does not encrypt queries, and it works only as a chain: Cloud DNS signs the zone, the registrar must publish a matching DS record in the parent zone, and the client's resolver must validate. A zone that shows DNSSEC as on but has no DS record at the registrar protects nobody. Response policies override answers inside a VPC network. A wildcard rule for *.malware-campaign.test can return a sinkhole address, and a passthru rule exempts one required subdomain so it resolves normally. Only one response policy can be attached to a network, but it can hold many rules. Query logging is switched on through a DNS policy on the network and records the names resolved by VMs, GKE containers and on-premises clients using inbound forwarding, written to Cloud Logging under the project that owns the network. That is where DNS tunnelling shows up as random-looking names, because flow logs record IP connections and audit logs record API calls. Routing policies steer traffic and are not a security control.

concepts.heading: Restricting and Monitoring API Use
concepts.body: The Restrict Resource Service Usage constraint, constraints/gcp.restrictServiceUsage, allows or denies Google Cloud services for an organization, folder or project, either as a denylist or as an allowlist but not both. It does not apply to essential dependencies such as IAM, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring, and services that depend directly on a restricted service are restricted too: denying Compute Engine also stops GKE. The effect is immediate, so Google suggests enforcing it conditionally with tags and widening scope gradually. The second control is the API key. A standard key identifies a project for quota and billing, not a principal, so IAM cannot limit who uses it, and a key embedded in a published Android app should be assumed extractable. Use two restrictions together. An API restriction limits the key to listed APIs, for example only the Places API. An application restriction limits where the key is accepted: websites by HTTP referrer, IP addresses, Android apps by package name and signing certificate fingerprint, or iOS apps by bundle identifier. A key with no application restriction works from anywhere. Review usage metrics and quota consumption per key to notice abuse.

examPoints: A question where private VMs still become reachable after IPv4 external addresses were denied points to the constraint covering IPv4 only, so the fix is internal IPv6 access plus ingress deny rules.

A question that allows one URL path and blocks another over HTTPS points to Secure Web Proxy with TLS inspection, and one about update clients that reject the proxy certificate points to session matcher exclusions.

A question about DNS lookups of random-looking names points to query logging through a DNS policy, one about a sinkhole with one exempted subdomain points to a response policy with passthru, and one about an embedded mobile key points to API and application restrictions.

quiz.q: A bank's managed VMs must download packages from www.example.com/documentation, but traffic to www.example.com/uploads must be blocked, and both are HTTPS requests leaving the VPC. Which design works?
choices: Secure Web Proxy without decryption, with a host rule for www.example.com that the proxy applies to each request path
A Cloud NGFW egress rule from the Standard tier that matches the FQDN object for www.example.com and then filters the path
A Cloud DNS response policy that returns a sinkhole address only for requests made to the uploads path on that host
Secure Web Proxy with TLS inspection from a CA Service pool, the root trusted on the VMs, and URL rules
quiz.explain: Without decryption an HTTPS request exposes only the host name, so a rule on the path is possible only after the proxy terminates TLS and inspects the request. That needs a certificate issued from a private CA that the managed VMs trust. A host rule cannot tell the two paths apart, an FQDN object matches names and not paths, and DNS answers are keyed by name, never by URL path.

quiz.q: Security operations suspects that a compromised GKE workload leaks data through DNS lookups of random-looking names resolved inside the VPC network. Flow logs only show connections to the resolver. What gives visibility into the names?
choices: VPC Flow Logs on the cluster subnet with a higher sampling rate, since the logs also record the names being resolved
Query logging enabled by a Cloud DNS policy on the VPC network, with entries read in Cloud Logging
Cloud Audit Logs Data Access entries for Cloud DNS, because they record each lookup made by a workload in the network
A Cloud DNS routing policy with geolocation records on the zone, which tags each lookup with the name that was queried
quiz.explain: Cloud DNS query logging, switched on by a DNS policy on the network, records the queries the network's resolver handles, including those from GKE containers, and writes them to Cloud Logging where sinks and alerts can use them. Flow logs record IP connections, not names, even when sampled more. Audit logs record API calls, not lookups. Routing policies steer answers and add no query visibility.

days.recap: Keep workloads private with two independent controls (no external address, no admitting firewall rule), send outbound web traffic through Secure Web Proxy, protect and log DNS, and limit Google API use with the service usage constraint and restricted API keys.

days.title: VPC Service Controls: Perimeters, Access Levels, Ingress and Egress Rules, Dry Run

concepts.heading: What a Perimeter Protects
concepts.body: A VPC Service Controls perimeter surrounds projects, and optionally VPC networks, so that the Google-managed services you list as restricted, such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery, cannot exchange data with anything outside it. It is a layer independent of IAM: IAM says who may call, while the perimeter says from where and toward which projects. That is why it helps when credentials are stolen, when a misconfigured IAM policy exposes a dataset, or when an insider or compromised code tries to copy data out. Service operations such as gcloud storage cp to a public bucket or bq mk to an external BigQuery table are blocked at the boundary. A firewall cannot do this, because every bucket, including an attacker's, sits behind the same storage.googleapis.com endpoint. In enforced mode violations are denied. Access from the internet is denied by default, and the Google Cloud console is blocked until an access level admits it. The service complements IAM and does not replace it.

concepts.heading: Access Levels and Ingress Rules
concepts.body: Two mechanisms admit requests from outside. An access level, created in Access Context Manager, classifies a request by attributes such as source IP range, region, identity and device policy. Device data comes from Endpoint Verification, with criteria such as screen lock, storage encryption and operating system version, and conditions in one level are combined, so a request must satisfy all of them. Analysts on changing home addresses suit a device-policy level better than IP ranges. An ingress rule is more granular. Its from block names identities and sources (an access level, a project or a VPC network), and its to block names services, methods or permissions and target projects. A partner's service account that must read one BigQuery dataset gets a rule that names that identity, the read methods and the owning project, instead of a level that admits a whole address range. A developer VM in an unprotected project that is blocked from a protected bucket needs an ingress rule with the caller's project as the source, because a private IP address alone is ambiguous. Ingress and egress rules replace many cases that once needed perimeter bridges.

concepts.heading: Egress, Shared VPC and Accessible Services
concepts.body: Direction describes the request, not the data flow. A VM inside the perimeter that writes a nightly export to an auditor's bucket is egress, so an egress rule must name that service account, the target project and the object-creation methods, and every other copy to an outside bucket stays blocked. Access levels and ingress rules never authorize a call that leaves the perimeter. A request touching resources on both sides can need both rule types. An analyst outside the perimeter who runs a BigQuery job in an outside project against a dataset inside needs an ingress rule for the analyst and an egress rule for the outside job project, and the audit log shows both violations when one is missing. Shared VPC adds a trap: VMs in service projects use the host project's network, so put the host project in the same perimeter, or requests look as if they come from a network outside it. VPC accessible services limits what endpoints inside the perimeter may call, for example only Cloud Storage and BigQuery. A call to anything else is denied and logged as SERVICE_NOT_ALLOWED_FROM_VPC.

concepts.heading: Dry Run and Access Policies
concepts.body: A new restriction can break workloads, so test it in dry run. A perimeter holds an enforced configuration and a dry run configuration. Dry run violations are logged with metadata.dryRun set to true and are not denied. The dry run configuration starts as a copy of the enforced one, and only requests that the enforced configuration allows but the dry run configuration would deny appear as dry run violations. Access levels have no dry run mode, so to test a change you create a new access level and attach it only to the dry run configuration. A project can be in one enforced and one dry run configuration, not necessarily of the same perimeter. To trial moving a project from perimeter PA to PB, remove it from PA's dry run configuration and add it to PB's. Read denials in the audit log by violationReason: NETWORK_NOT_IN_SAME_SERVICE_PERIMETER points to an ingress or egress rule for a network, and NO_MATCHING_ACCESS_LEVEL to an internet caller that matched nothing. An organization has one organization-level access policy, and scoped policies let a business unit manage its own folder.

examPoints: A question about copying data to a bucket in an attacker's project, despite correct IAM and firewall rules, points to a VPC Service Controls perimeter, because only it checks which project owns the resource being called.

A question that shares one dataset with a partner points to an identity-based ingress rule with narrow methods and target project, and one about a VM writing to an auditor's bucket points to a narrow egress rule.

A question about testing a new restricted service or access level before enforcing points to the dry run configuration with a new access level, and one about Shared VPC failures points to the host project joining the perimeter.

quiz.q: A perimeter is enforced around analytics projects. The team wants to add the Cloud KMS API as a restricted service and admit requests from a new office network, and must see what would break before any user is affected. What should they do?
choices: Edit the existing access level in place and turn on its dry run mode, then read the violations it logs for the perimeter
Change the enforced configuration at once, because the audit log reports requests that were denied and can be reverted
Create a second perimeter for the same projects in enforced mode, and keep both until the denied requests are compared
Change the dry run configuration, add a new access level for the office to it, and review the logged dry run violations
quiz.explain: A dry run configuration can be changed freely without affecting enforcement, and its violations are logged with the dry run flag. Access levels have no dry run mode of their own, so the change is made as a new access level attached to the dry run configuration. Editing the enforced configuration affects users immediately. A project can be in only one enforced configuration, so a second enforced perimeter is not possible.

quiz.q: A research partner's service account in the partner's own organization must read one BigQuery dataset in a project inside an enforced perimeter. What is the most precise, least-privilege way to allow it?
choices: An access level admitting the partner's published IP ranges, attached to the perimeter for every restricted service
An ingress rule naming that service account, the BigQuery read methods and the owning project as the target
A perimeter bridge joining the partner's project to the perimeter, so projects on both sides can reach each other
An egress rule that lets the dataset's project call the partner's project for the BigQuery read operations
quiz.explain: An ingress rule can be narrowed by identity, method and target project, so only that account gets only read access to one project regardless of its source address. An access level admits by attributes such as IP range and is far broader. Perimeter bridges are bidirectional and cannot include projects from different organizations. Egress describes requests leaving the perimeter, which is the wrong direction for this call.

days.recap: A VPC Service Controls perimeter is the control for data exfiltration through Google APIs: admit outsiders with narrow ingress rules, allow exits with narrow egress rules, keep Shared VPC host and service projects together, and test every change in dry run.

days.title: Segmentation: VPC Security Properties, Peering, Shared VPC, Firewall Rules and N-tier Isolation

concepts.heading: VPC Building Blocks and Defaults
concepts.body: A VPC network is a global resource and its subnets are regional. Auto mode networks create one subnet in every region from predefined ranges inside 10.128.0.0/9, while custom mode networks contain only the subnets you define, so you can plan ranges that do not overlap with peered or on-premises networks. Two auto mode networks cannot even be peered, because their ranges collide. Every network has two implied rules at the lowest priority: allow all egress and deny all ingress. The default network that a new project receives also comes with pre-populated rules that allow certain ingress traffic. Enforcing constraints/compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation on a folder skips creating that default network and its supporting resources, so teams build custom mode networks with explicit rules instead. A sound checklist for a new project is therefore no default network, custom mode subnets, explicit allow rules between tiers, and organization policy against external IPs and IP forwarding. The implied deny ingress is the safety net, not the design: write the rules you intend, so the allowed paths are visible and auditable.

concepts.heading: N-tier Isolation
concepts.body: Segmentation between web, application and database tiers comes from allowing only adjacent tiers to talk: web to app on the app port, app to database on the database port, and everything else falls to the implied deny. Write sources and targets as service accounts or secure tags rather than IP ranges, so rules follow the workload when it scales or moves. Secure tags in network firewall policies are the micro-segmentation tool, and hierarchical firewall policies set guardrails above the projects. Rule actions decide who has the last word: allow and deny stop evaluation, and goto_next delegates downward. A relay path is another way around tiers. When IP forwarding is enabled, a VM can forward packets for other addresses, so the Restrict VM IP forwarding constraint, constraints/compute.managed.vmCanIpForward, denies it for a folder, and approved network appliances get an override on their own project. Firewall rules match packet addresses and ports and cannot know that a VM is acting as a relay. Finally, firewalls cannot separate a company bucket from an attacker's bucket, because both are the same API endpoint. That boundary belongs to VPC Service Controls.

concepts.heading: VPC Network Peering
concepts.body: VPC Network Peering joins two networks over internal addresses but keeps them administratively separate. Only routes are exchanged, according to each side's settings, and firewall rules and policies are not. Peering is not transitive: if net-a peers with net-b and with net-c, there is no path between net-b and net-c. Each network enforces its own implied deny ingress, so a database network that wants only the application subnet 10.20.0.0/24 on tcp:5432 writes one ingress allow rule with that source range. Egress to the peer needs no rule unless a deny exists. Network tags and service accounts in VPC firewall rules resolve only to instances in the rule's own network, so a peer's tag never matches. Use the peer's IP range instead, or a secure tag as the source in a network firewall policy, which can identify sources in the tag's network and in networks peered with it. By default a network admin can peer with any other network, so the Restrict VPC peering usage constraint, constraints/compute.restrictVpcPeering, lists the networks that may be peered, for example everything under the organization. It acts before the peering exists, unlike an audit alert.

concepts.heading: Shared VPC and Separation of Duties
concepts.body: Shared VPC fits one organization that wants central control of the network and delegated compute administration. A host project owns the Shared VPC network, service projects attach to it and each service project has a single host. A project cannot be both host and service, and participating projects must belong to the same organization. Roles split the duties. The Shared VPC Admin enables host projects and attaches service projects. Network Admin on the host project controls network resources except firewall rules and SSL certificates. Security Admin on the host project manages firewall rules and SSL certificates. Service project admins hold Compute Network User on specific subnets and can create instances without changing the network. Granting that role per subnet instead of on the whole host project gives each team its own slice. Two constraints add guardrails: constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcHostProjects limits which hosts a project, folder or organization can attach to, and constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcSubnetworks limits which shared subnets service projects may use for new VMs and load balancers. Choose Shared VPC for central administration and peering where networks stay separately administered.

examPoints: A question about a peer network's tag that never matches points to firewall rules resolving tags and service accounts only inside their own network, so the rule needs the peer's IP range or a secure tag as source.

A question about stopping teams from peering with outside networks before the connection exists points to the Restrict VPC peering usage constraint, and one about new projects with permissive default rules points to skipping default network creation.

A question about separating who manages routes from who manages firewall rules in Shared VPC points to Network Admin and Security Admin on the host project, with Compute Network User granted per subnet.

quiz.q: Two peered networks, net-app and net-db, host the application and database tiers. An administrator of net-db wrote an ingress allow rule for tcp:5432 whose source is the network tag app-tier, yet application VMs in net-app cannot connect. What fixes this with the least exposure?
choices: Use the application subnet's range as source, since network tags resolve only inside the rule's own network
Create the same app-tier tag on the database VMs, because peered networks share tags through the peering configuration
Add an egress allow rule in net-app for tcp:5432, because the implied egress rule is removed by peering for those VMs
Allow tcp:5432 from 0.0.0.0/0 in net-db, because peering already restricts traffic to the two peered networks
quiz.explain: Network tags in a VPC firewall rule resolve only to instances in the rule's own network, so the peer's tag matches nothing. A rule with the application subnet's range as source admits exactly that tier. Peering does not share tags or merge firewall rules, and egress is allowed by the implied rule unless an egress deny exists. Opening the port to every address gives up the segmentation that the design was meant to deliver.

quiz.q: A company runs Shared VPC and wants network administrators to control subnets and routes, but only the security team to change firewall rules and SSL certificates. Which grant on the host project does this?
choices: Shared VPC Admin for both teams, because that role is the only one that manages firewall rules in a host project
Compute Network User for both teams on every shared subnet, with firewall rules left at the project defaults
Network Admin for the network team and Security Admin for the security team, both granted on the host project
Network Admin for both teams on the host project, because it already covers firewall rules and SSL certificates
quiz.explain: Network Admin has full control of network resources except firewall rules and SSL certificates, and Security Admin is the role that manages those, so splitting the two roles separates the duties. Shared VPC Admin enables host projects and attaches service projects, and it is not meant for daily firewall work. Compute Network User only lets a team use subnets. Network Admin deliberately excludes firewall rules.

days.recap: Segment with custom mode networks, tier-to-tier allow rules based on service accounts or secure tags, and organization policy guardrails, then choose peering for separately administered networks and Shared VPC for central control with split Network and Security Admin duties.

days.title: Private Connectivity: Private Google Access, Private Service Connect, HA VPN, Interconnect and Cloud NAT

concepts.heading: Private Google Access, Private and Restricted Ranges
concepts.body: A VM with only an internal address reaches Google APIs when Private Google Access is enabled on its subnet (a per-subnet setting that does not affect VMs with external addresses). On-premises hosts take another path: they send API traffic to a virtual IP range over Cloud VPN or VLAN attachments, and the subnet setting is not needed. Two domains exist. private.googleapis.com, 199.36.153.8/30, reaches most Google APIs, including ones that VPC Service Controls does not support. restricted.googleapis.com, 199.36.153.4/30, reaches only APIs that VPC Service Controls supports, so a regulated client cannot fall back to an unprotected API. DNS chooses the range, and each client population should resolve to exactly one of them, because mixed answers cause intermittent failures. Google publishes no routes for these ranges, so Cloud Router advertises the range to on premises as a custom advertised route, and the VPC network needs a custom static route to it with the default internet gateway as next hop. It restores access to just that range if the default route was deleted. Responses return through attachments in the region of the request, so keep attachments in each such region.

concepts.heading: Private Service Connect
concepts.body: Private Service Connect gives private access to services through addresses you control. An endpoint for Google APIs is a forwarding rule with an internal IP address in your VPC network that maps to an API bundle: all-apis, or vpc-sc for the services VPC Service Controls supports.
