Unlike Private Google Access you choose the address and can create one per team, and on-premises hosts reach it over Cloud VPN or VLAN attachments. DNS decides whether it is used. The endpoint creates names such as storage-logs1.p.googleapis.com in a private zone, and a client whose lookup misses that zone falls through to public DNS and connects publicly. Backends put your own load balancer in front of a service attachment or Google API, which gives custom domains and certificates, Cloud Armor and control of regional failover. For Google-managed services such as Cloud SQL, an endpoint avoids the allocated range and VPC Network Peering of private services access, and peering is not transitive. A producer's service attachment can accept connections only from an accept list. A connection stays Pending, with no traffic flowing, when its project is not on the accept list or when the connections exceed the service attachment's connection limit.

concepts.heading: Encrypting Hybrid Links: HA VPN and MACsec
concepts.body: Cloud VPN protects traffic with IPsec, and its tunnels cross the public internet. HA VPN uses dynamic routing with BGP. Cloud Interconnect gives a private path, but encryption is something you add, and the two options work at different layers. MACsec for Cloud Interconnect, IEEE 802.1AE, encrypts at layer 2 between your on-premises router and Google's edge routers, using keys you configure on your router. It does not provide encryption in transit within Google, so Google recommends layering it with IPsec and TLS. On Partner Interconnect the provider's network is in the path, so MACsec has to be arranged with the service provider. When a policy asks for network-layer encryption end to end between your networks and the VPC, use HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect: IPsec tunnels over the VLAN attachments, which keep the private Interconnect path and give layer 3 encryption. A retailer with Dedicated Interconnect and that policy chooses HA VPN over Interconnect, and an enterprise that only needs the link between routers protected can choose MACsec. The two can be combined for defense in depth.

concepts.heading: Cloud NAT for Controlled Egress
concepts.body: Cloud NAT gives resources without external IP addresses outbound access to internet destinations. It is a distributed, software-defined service configured on a Cloud Router, with no proxy VMs or appliances in the path. A gateway translates only the subnets or subnet ranges you select, so scope it to the subnets that need it. In a project with build VMs and sensitive data-processing VMs, a gateway serving only the build subnet leaves the sensitive VMs with no external address and no translation, and the external IP constraint stops anyone adding one by mistake. Cloud NAT translates established inbound response packets only and never allows unsolicited inbound connections. Many VMs share a few external addresses, so a partner reporting scanning from one cannot name the VM. Cloud NAT logging in Cloud Logging, set to record translations, ties the external address and port to the internal VM. Logging only errors would miss connections that succeeded.  The Restrict Cloud NAT usage constraint, constraints/compute.restrictCloudNATUsage, limits which subnetworks may use Cloud NAT.

examPoints: A question where on-premises clients must reach only Google APIs that VPC Service Controls protects points to restricted.googleapis.com resolved by on-premises DNS and advertised through Cloud Router, and one with intermittent failures points to DNS mixing the two ranges.

A question about an internal address from the consumer's own subnet for a Google API or a managed service points to a Private Service Connect endpoint, and one where the endpoint exists but traffic goes public points to a missing private DNS answer.

A question about network-layer encryption over Dedicated Interconnect points to HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, one about protecting only the hop between routers points to MACsec, and one about tracing a shared NAT address points to Cloud NAT translation logging.

quiz.q: An insurer's on-premises servers call Cloud Storage and BigQuery over HA VPN tunnels. VPC Service Controls protects the data projects, and the servers must be unable to reach any Google API that VPC Service Controls cannot protect. Which design meets this?
choices: Resolve Google API names to private.googleapis.com on premises and advertise that range from the Cloud Router
Resolve Google API names to restricted.googleapis.com on premises and advertise that range from the Cloud Router
Enable Private Google Access on the subnets that end the tunnels, since it also covers requests from on premises
Give each server a public route to Google APIs, then deny external requests with VPC Service Controls ingress rules
quiz.explain: The restricted range serves only the APIs that VPC Service Controls supports, so unprotected APIs become unreachable, and advertising it from Cloud Router keeps the traffic on the tunnels. The private range reaches most APIs, including unprotected ones. For on-premises hosts the subnet setting is not what makes access work. A public route leaves the internet path open.

quiz.q: A retailer uses Dedicated Interconnect. A new policy requires all traffic between its on-premises networks and the VPC networks to be encrypted at the network layer, end to end. What should the network team deploy?
choices: MACsec on the Dedicated Interconnect ports, which encrypts traffic from the on-premises router into the VPC
A Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs, which wraps each connection to the VPC in a private tunnel
Cloud NAT on the VPC subnets, which translates addresses so that on-premises traffic appears from a new range
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, with IPsec tunnels built across the VLAN attachments of the existing links
quiz.explain: IPsec tunnels over the VLAN attachments give layer 3 encryption between the networks while keeping the private path. MACsec works at layer 2 between the on-premises router and Google's edge routers and does not provide encryption in transit within Google. A Private Service Connect endpoint is an address for reaching a service and does not encrypt a link. Cloud NAT only translates addresses.

days.recap: Reach Google APIs and managed services privately with Private Google Access ranges (restricted for VPC Service Controls) or Private Service Connect endpoints, encrypt hybrid links with HA VPN over Interconnect or MACsec, and scope Cloud NAT to the subnets that need egress.

days.title: Sensitive Data Protection: Discovery, Inspection, Redaction and Tokenization

concepts.heading: Three Jobs: Discover, Inspect, De-identify
concepts.body: Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP; the API is still called the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API) does three different jobs, and exam scenarios hinge on picking the right one. Discovery is continuous: it monitors an organization, folder or project, classifies data into infoTypes and calculates sensitivity and data risk levels. Inspection is a request-time scan of specific content that returns findings. De-identification is a transformation that changes the content, for example by redacting, masking or tokenizing a value. A bank that asks where its national ID numbers live across 400 projects needs discovery, because only discovery covers many projects without a job per table. A team that must hand a text export to a vendor needs inspection plus de-identification. A common trap is to expect discovery to modify data: it classifies and assesses, and it never changes files or tables. Choose the job from the verb in the requirement: find continuously, find in this content, or change this content.

concepts.heading: Discovery Profiles and Actions
concepts.body: A discovery scan configuration sets the scope, the inspection template that lists the infoTypes, and the actions to take after each scan. For BigQuery and Cloud SQL the service produces one table profile per table, one column profile per column and one project profile per scanned project; for Cloud Storage it produces one file store profile per bucket. BigQuery tables are scanned in place through the BigQuery Storage Read API, so no export or copy is needed, and non-BigLake external tables such as Google Sheets and BigQuery Omni tables are not supported. Actions include sending profiles to Security Command Center, which surfaces high-risk data, and publishing a Pub/Sub notification when a profile's sensitivity level changes, which can trigger automation. A separate secrets discovery looks at environment variables of Cloud Run functions and service revisions and reports findings to Security Command Center without generating data profiles. The follow-up fix is to move such secrets into Secret Manager.

concepts.heading: Tuning Inspection and Redacting Images
concepts.body: Inspection finds values by infoType: built-in detectors, custom regular expressions or custom dictionaries. Two noisy-results problems have different cures. When a built-in detector flags order numbers such as ORD-48213 as national IDs, add an exclusion rule that drops findings matching that pattern. When company-specific employee codes are never found, add a custom infoType with a regular expression. Hotword rules raise or lower likelihood when a word appears near a match, and a minimum likelihood setting filters weak matches; lowering that setting makes noise worse, not better. Changing data afterwards, for example by hashing, does not improve detection. For pictures, image redaction uses optical character recognition to find text and can also detect certain objects, and it returns a new image with opaque rectangles over the matches. An insurer sharing claim photos with a vendor lists infoTypes such as PERSON_NAME and the licence plate object type. Character masking works on text, not pixels.

concepts.heading: Choosing a De-identification Transformation
concepts.body: The transformations fall into two groups. Redaction deletes a value and masking overwrites characters; neither can be reversed, and neither keeps records linkable. Cryptographic hashing is also one-way, but the same input and key always give the same output, so tables can still be joined. The reversible pair is AES-SIV and FPE-FFX. AES-SIV (deterministic encryption) accepts any characters and any length and gives the same token for the same input, so it suits email addresses. FPE-FFX keeps the length and a chosen alphabet for legacy systems that validate format, but needs short values of uniform length. Reversal needs the same key, so use a Cloud KMS wrapped key, which the documentation prefers. A transient key is discarded after the request and cannot support re-identification later. A context tweak mixes another column, such as a campaign ID, into the token so equal inputs differ across contexts. For free text, a surrogate annotation is required to find tokens again.

examPoints: A question that asks for continuous classification and risk levels across many projects, with an alert when sensitivity changes, points to organization-level discovery with Security Command Center and Pub/Sub actions rather than one-off inspection jobs.

A question that needs tokens an authorized pipeline can reverse later, with the same token for the same input, points to AES-SIV or FPE-FFX with a Cloud KMS wrapped key, and a question that needs the token to stay the same length and alphabet points to FPE-FFX.

A question about hiding names and licence plates in photos points to image redaction with infoTypes, while a question that must stop linkage of the same person across datasets points to a context tweak.

quiz.q: A data team tokenizes customer email addresses (varying lengths, any characters) in BigQuery. Analysts must join records for the same customer, and a privacy office must be able to reverse tokens later. Which transformation fits?
choices: Cryptographic hashing with a key, so equal inputs give equal outputs and joins still work
Character masking of the local part, so the domain stays visible for analytics grouping
Deterministic encryption with AES-SIV using a Cloud KMS wrapped key shared across runs
Format-preserving encryption over a numeric alphabet, so every token has the same shape
quiz.explain: AES-SIV accepts any characters and lengths, gives the same token for the same input and can be reversed with the key. Hashing keeps joins working but is one-way, masking is irreversible, and a numeric alphabet cannot represent email addresses.

quiz.q: A security team must learn when any BigQuery table across 400 projects becomes more sensitive, for example when a column starts holding national ID numbers, and must see high-risk tables centrally. What should it do?
choices: Schedule an inspection job on every table in every project each night and email the findings
Enable Data Access audit logs on BigQuery and search them for reads of any sensitive columns
Configure organization discovery with actions to Security Command Center and Pub/Sub notifications
Redact the national ID column in every project so that no table can become more sensitive over time
quiz.explain: Discovery profiles data continuously across the scope, calculates sensitivity and risk, and can notify on changes. Per-table inspection jobs do not scale to 400 projects, audit logs record access and not content, and redaction changes data rather than monitoring it.

days.recap: Discovery finds and monitors, inspection locates values, and de-identification changes them: only AES-SIV and FPE-FFX with a stable Cloud KMS wrapped key can be reversed.

days.title: Restricting Data Access: BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Secret Manager and Metadata

concepts.heading: BigQuery: Scope the Data Role, Share Through Views
concepts.body: Running a query takes two permissions: creating jobs (BigQuery Job User on the project that runs the query) and reading the data. Granting Data Viewer at the project covers every dataset, now and future, so an analyst group that should read two curated datasets gets Data Viewer on those datasets and only the job role on the project. To share a subset, publish an authorized view. A view runs with its own access to the source, so analysts need Data Viewer on the dataset holding the view, and the view is added to the source dataset's authorized views; source and view datasets must be in the same region. Without the authorization the query fails with access denied. When a central team keeps 40 views over three source datasets, an authorized dataset needs one grant per source and covers current and future views. The trade-off is that anyone who can create a view in that dataset can read the source, so control who can create views there.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage and Cloud SQL: Narrow Roles and Guardrails
concepts.body: Pick the narrowest object role. Storage Object Creator can add objects but cannot view, overwrite or delete them, which fits an ingestion account whose stolen credentials must not touch existing data. Storage Object User can create, overwrite, delete and read, and legacy bucket roles carry object permissions that can break least privilege. Pair grants with versioning, soft delete or a retention policy. Organization policy turns conventions into guardrails: storage.publicAccessPrevention blocks allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers, and iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains limits which identities can enter IAM policies. Uniform bucket-level access ends ACLs but still allows IAM grants to anyone. For Cloud SQL, sql.restrictPublicIp and sql.restrictAuthorizedNetworks are not retroactive: instances that already have a public IP keep it, so find them with inventory or Security Command Center findings and remove the exposure. To drop long-lived database passwords, use IAM database authentication, where the Cloud SQL connector or Auth Proxy supplies short-lived tokens and logins are attributable to a service account.

concepts.heading: Secret Manager: Versions, Rotation and Residency
concepts.body: Secret Manager is the place for credentials, and the controls are about who reads, which version and where. Grant Secret Manager Secret Accessor on a single secret, not on the project, and never Version Manager to a consumer that only reads. Google recommends referencing secrets by version number and deploying changes through your release process. The latest alias moves to the newest enabled version, so a faulty new version can break every instance that starts afterwards. Disable a version before destroying it, because a disabled version is reversible and looks the same as destroyed to consumers. A rotation schedule does not change any credential: at the next rotation time Secret Manager publishes a SECRET_ROTATE message to the configured Pub/Sub topic, and a subscriber you build must create the new credential and add the version. For strict residency, regional secrets stay in their location at rest, in use and in transit and can be accessed only from that location, whereas global secrets are replicated by policy and readable from any region.

concepts.heading: Instance Metadata, OS Login and GKE Workload Identity
concepts.body: Every Compute Engine VM can query its metadata server without extra authorization, and the server also issues access tokens for the attached service account. Any process that can reach the metadata URL sees every value, so a server-side request forgery bug in a web app can leak the token. Reduce its value with a dedicated user-managed service account holding minimal roles, and validate or block internal destinations in code. Metadata is not a secret store: custom values are readable to processes on the VM and to principals who can view instance or project metadata, so keep passwords in Secret Manager and grant the VM's service account access to that secret. SSH keys in project metadata let a metadata editor log in everywhere; OS Login ties SSH to IAM roles with audit, and the compute.managed.requireOsLogin constraint prevents metadata updates that disable it. On GKE, pods can reach the node's metadata server and obtain the node account's token; Workload Identity Federation for GKE answers with the workload's own Kubernetes identity instead.

examPoints: A question where analysts must query a subset of a table without access to the source dataset points to an authorized view, and one with dozens of views over several source datasets points to an authorized dataset.
A question about an organization policy that was enforced but old Cloud SQL instances are still public points to constraints not being retroactive, so existing exposure must be found and removed.

A question about a rotation job that did nothing, or a password stored in instance metadata, points to a Pub/Sub subscriber that creates versions and to Secret Manager read by the VM's own service account.

quiz.q: Analysts hold BigQuery Data Viewer at the project level, so they can read payroll. They should read only two curated datasets and still run queries in the project. Which fix follows least privilege?
choices: Keep Data Viewer on the project and add a row-level access policy on the payroll tables only
Grant Data Viewer on the two datasets, drop it at project level, and keep BigQuery Job User
Move the payroll dataset to another folder so that folder-level inheritance no longer applies to it
Replace Data Viewer with BigQuery User at the project so analysts can only run their own jobs
quiz.explain: The data role belongs at dataset level and only the job role at project level. Row policies leave table reads inherited, datasets stay in the same project when folders change, and BigQuery User does not remove the inherited read access.

quiz.q: A nightly service account must add log files to a bucket. If its credentials are stolen, it must not be able to read, overwrite or delete existing objects. Which grant fits?
choices: Storage Object User on the bucket, with a retention policy added for protection
Storage Object Viewer plus a legacy bucket writer role limited to one prefix
Storage Admin with an IAM condition that limits the account to one object prefix
Storage Object Creator on the bucket, with versioning enabled as a safety net
quiz.explain: Object Creator allows creating objects only, with no view, overwrite or delete. Object User can overwrite, delete and read, Viewer allows reads and the legacy writer role includes delete, and a prefix condition on Storage Admin still allows deleting within the prefix.

days.recap: Put data roles at the narrowest scope, share subsets through authorized views, make guardrails with organization policy while remembering they are not retroactive, and keep secrets in Secret Manager rather than metadata.

days.title: Encryption at Rest: CMEK, EKM, HSM Keys, Rotation, Import and Autokey

concepts.heading: Default Encryption Versus CMEK
concepts.body: Google Cloud encrypts customer content at rest by default using envelope encryption: data encryption keys are wrapped by key encryption keys in Google's internal key management service, with no configuration. With customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) the key encryption key is a Cloud KMS key you control, so you choose its location and rotation, see key operations in audit logs, and can disable or destroy key versions to cut off use of the data. That cut-off is real: when a Cloud SQL instance cannot access its key, for example because a version was disabled, Cloud SQL suspends the instance and resumes it automatically once the key is accessible again. CMEK does not add encryption that was missing, does not replace TLS, and does not stop an authorized principal who may read through the service, because the service decrypts on the caller's behalf. Good reasons for CMEK are control over key location and rotation, audit of key use, and the ability to revoke the service's access.

concepts.heading: Protection Levels and Cloud EKM
concepts.body: A key's protection level is fixed at creation and all versions share it. SOFTWARE runs in software, HSM uses Cloud HSM (multi-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware managed by Google), HSM_SINGLE_TENANT gives dedicated partitions that the customer administers, and EXTERNAL or EXTERNAL_VPC keep the key in a supported external key manager. Each Cloud HSM key has an attestation statement signed by the hardware, which an auditor can verify. Because the level cannot change, moving from software to hardware means a new key and re-protecting data; existing Cloud Storage objects keep their old key until rewritten. With Cloud EKM, key material never leaves the external manager, and every operation calls it, so you can revoke access at any time, but partner downtime becomes an outage and Google cannot recover data if the external key is lost. EXTERNAL reaches the manager over the internet; EXTERNAL_VPC uses a VPC network and is positioned for better availability. A manually managed external key cannot rotate on a schedule; a coordinated external key (EXTERNAL_VPC, managed from Cloud KMS) can for symmetric encryption.

concepts.heading: Rotation, Versions and Destruction
concepts.body: Rotating a symmetric key creates a new version and makes it primary for new encryption. It does not re-encrypt existing data and does not disable older versions, which keep decrypting. After a suspected exposure of an old version the sequence is: rotate, re-encrypt data under the new primary version, confirm nothing depends on the old version, then disable it and schedule destruction. A disabled version can be re-enabled, a version in the scheduled-for-destruction state can be restored during the destruction period (30 days by default), and a destroyed version is gone for good. The destruction duration can be set only at key creation, between 24 hours and 120 days, so a tenant contract requiring faster erasure needs the key created that way. Asymmetric keys do not support automatic rotation: for signing keys you distribute the new public key before switching, so script it. IAM cannot be set on a key version, and rotation creates versions over time, so per-tenant access and crypto-shredding need one key per tenant.

concepts.heading: Importing Key Material and Autokey
concepts.body: When policy says key material must originate in your own HSM, import it. Create a target key (skipping the initial version if your material should be version 1), create an import job with a protection level and an RSA wrapping method, wrap the key locally with the job's public key, and send it; an import job expires after three days. Protection level and location cannot change after import. Imported keys have automatic rotation disabled by default, because rotation would make Cloud KMS generate material itself; the import-only setting stops Cloud KMS from generating any version, so new material arrives through new import jobs. Cloud KMS Autokey automates CMEK at scale. When a developer creates a supported resource, the Autokey service agent creates the key ring and key on demand, in the same location as the resource, and grants the service account use of it. Keys are HSM-protected AES-256 GCM with a one-year default rotation that an administrator can edit. Developers can only request keys, while administrators manage them without encrypt or decrypt permission.

examPoints: A question that demands proof that keys are generated and used in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware points to Cloud HSM keys with their attestation statements, not to software keys or Cloud EKM.

A question where an exposed old key version still decrypts data after a rotation points to re-encrypting data and then disabling and destroying that version, because rotation alone does not retire older versions.

A question about key material that must start in the company's own HSM points to key import with the import-only setting, and one about scheduled rotation of an external key points to a coordinated external key managed from Cloud KMS, because a manually managed external key cannot rotate automatically.

quiz.q: A security engineer rotated a symmetric Cloud KMS key after an old version was exposed. A red team shows the old version still decrypts stored data. What is the correct response?
choices: Re-encrypt data under the new primary version, then disable and destroy the old version
Rotate again on a much shorter schedule so that the old version is replaced by the newest one
Change the protection level of the key to HSM so that all of its older versions stop working
Delete the key from its key ring and recreate it with the same name for the application
quiz.explain: Rotation makes a new version primary but does not re-encrypt existing data or disable older versions. Rotating again changes nothing about the old version, protection level cannot be changed, and keys cannot be deleted and recreated like that.

quiz.q: A SaaS vendor must crypto-shred one tenant's data on offboarding and let each tenant's support group use only that tenant's data. Today one Cloud KMS key has a version per tenant. What should it do?
choices: Grant each support group access to its tenant's key version and destroy that version at offboarding
Create one key per tenant, set IAM on each key, and destroy that key's versions at offboarding
Put each tenant's key version in its own key ring and set IAM on the key ring for the group
Keep the single key and rotate it at each offboarding so that old tenant data becomes unreadable
quiz.explain: IAM cannot be set on a key version, and versions represent time rather than tenants, so independent access and erasure need one key per tenant. Key rings group keys but do not separate versions, and rotation never makes old data unreadable.

days.recap: CMEK gives control and a kill switch, protection level and location are fixed at creation, rotation never retires old versions by itself, and independent tenants need independent keys.

days.title: Encryption in Transit and in Use: SSL Policies, Service Mesh, Confidential Computing and Lifecycle

concepts.heading: What Google Encrypts in Transit, and When
concepts.body: Google protects its own infrastructure by default: TLS at the front end, ALTS between Google services, and encryption of VM-to-VM connections inside its production network, including connections within a VPC network and across peered VPC networks. Hosts establish session keys over a control channel protected by ALTS, and the keys are rotated periodically. The catch is that this automatic encryption is activated by the use of internal IP addresses. Two VMs in peered networks that talk over their external IP addresses are not covered at the network layer, so an auditor will ask for application-level TLS or, better, a move onto the internal path, which also removes a public exposure. These defaults do not give workloads identity. When 40 microservices on GKE need every call authenticated in both directions, with certificates the company controls, the answer is Cloud Service Mesh with mutual TLS: policy is central, applications keep speaking plain protocols to their local proxy, and certificate issuance and rotation are handled by the mesh.

concepts.heading: SSL Policies on Load Balancers
concepts.body: An SSL policy defines the TLS features a load balancer supports during a handshake: protocol versions and cipher suites. It is attached to a target HTTPS proxy or target SSL proxy and affects only the leg from the client to the load balancer; the leg to the backend is configured on the backend service. The profile (COMPATIBLE, MODERN, RESTRICTED, FIPS_202205 or CUSTOM) sets the capabilities, and a minimum TLS version narrows them further. FIPS_202205 supports TLS capabilities intended to meet FIPS 140-3; for TLS 1.3 it supports two of the three cipher suites the other profiles offer. Load balancers do not support SSL 3.0 or earlier whatever the profile. The policy governs TLS over TCP: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which uses TLS 1.3 exclusively, so a client on HTTP/3 negotiates TLS 1.3 even when the policy sets a minimum of 1.2. An SSL policy is not attached to Cloud Armor, and it does not authenticate individual services; that is the mesh's job.

concepts.heading: Data in Use: Confidential Computing
concepts.body: Confidential VM protects data in use with hardware memory encryption inside a trusted execution environment, plus attestation. The technology depends on the CPU. AMD SEV encrypts memory with minimal performance cost and supports live migration on N2D and C3D. AMD SEV-SNP adds protection against a malicious hypervisor, such as data replay and memory remapping, and attestation reports on demand. Intel TDX provides an isolated trust domain and also defends against limited physical attacks on memory. SEV-SNP and TDX do not support live migration, so host maintenance can restart a VM: design for checkpoints and autohealing, or stay on SEV if the threat model allows. Confidential GKE Nodes can be enabled for the whole cluster at creation (irreversible), for a node pool, or per workload through a ComputeClass, which suits protecting only a few pods. NVIDIA Confidential Computing extends the environment to supported GPUs. A TEE guards against the platform, not against a flawed application inside the VM, and it does not replace disk or transport encryption. Confidential Space lets parties release keys only to an attested workload.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Lifecycle Rules and Retention
concepts.body: Object Lifecycle Management performs actions such as Delete, SetStorageClass and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload when conditions are met. A Delete does not take effect on an object that has a hold or an unfulfilled retention policy; it happens after the hold is removed or the retention ends. A locked retention policy is permanent, so retention is the mechanism for immutability and lifecycle rules are for cleanup afterward. When several rules match the same object at once, only one action runs: Delete takes precedence over SetStorageClass, and among SetStorageClass rules the class with the lowest at-rest storage price wins. Overlapping rules are a common cause of accidental deletion, so test on a development bucket or a prefix first. Incomplete multipart uploads leave parts in the bucket that nobody reviews; the abort action cleans them up and allows only age, matchesPrefix and matchesSuffix as conditions, and a rule that combines it with other conditions is rejected.

examPoints: A question where two VMs in peered networks communicate through external IP addresses and the auditor wants default network-layer encryption points to using internal addresses, while a question about mutual authentication between microservices with customer-managed certificates points to Cloud Service Mesh.

A question about protecting memory from a compromised hypervisor with replay and remapping attacks on AMD hardware points to Confidential VM with SEV-SNP, and one about only a few pods in an existing GKE cluster points to workload-level Confidential Nodes.
A question about a lifecycle delete rule on a bucket with a locked retention policy points to the retention policy winning, with deletion happening only after the period ends.

quiz.q: A bank attaches an SSL policy with a minimum TLS version of 1.2 to the target HTTPS proxy of its external Application Load Balancer. Auditors ask which TLS version HTTP/3 clients use. What is accurate?
choices: They negotiate TLS 1.3, because QUIC uses TLS 1.3 exclusively and the policy covers TLS over TCP
They negotiate TLS 1.2, because the minimum version in the policy applies to every client protocol
They fall back to TLS 1.1, because the RESTRICTED profile allows older versions on QUIC traffic
They are rejected, because an SSL policy blocks HTTP/3 until the profile is switched to MODERN
quiz.explain: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which uses TLS 1.3 exclusively, and SSL policy documentation applies to TLS over TCP. The other answers assume the policy governs QUIC or lowers versions, which it does not.

quiz.q: A bucket holds audit exports under a locked retention policy of seven years. A lifecycle rule deletes objects older than one year. What happens to a 13-month-old object?
choices: The rule is rejected at creation because a delete rule cannot coexist with a locked retention policy
The object is deleted at 13 months, because lifecycle rules run before retention is evaluated
The object moves to Archive storage first, and the delete runs after the retention period ends
The delete waits until the retention period is fulfilled, and only then can the rule remove it
quiz.explain: A Delete action does not take effect on an object whose retention policy is unfulfilled, and the deletion can happen afterwards. The rule is allowed, lifecycle does not override retention, and no automatic storage class move occurs.

days.recap: Default network encryption needs internal IPs, SSL policies tune only the client-to-load-balancer leg, Confidential Computing protects memory with trade-offs by technology, and retention always beats lifecycle deletion.

days.title: Securing AI Workloads: Privacy, Identity, Perimeters, Model Armor and Agents

concepts.heading: Privacy Controls and Zero Data Retention
concepts.body: The AI platform is now named Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; older pages and the API still say Vertex AI. For managed models, Google states it will not use your data to train or fine-tune models without your prior permission or instruction, for GA and pre-GA models alike. That is a training restriction, not zero data retention, and legal teams often confuse them. Retention can still come from several places: prompt and response logging for abuse monitoring on some advanced models, where zero retention may not be possible; Grounding with Google Search, which stores derived-query logs for up to three days; request-response logging, which is off by default and writes to a BigQuery table if enabled; and the Interactions API, which stores conversation state when store is true, and store defaults to true. A zero-retention design therefore sets store to false, leaves request-response logging off and avoids features that retain data. CMEK controls the keys of stored resources and does not change whether a feature retains data.

concepts.heading: IaaS or PaaS Training, and Which Identity Runs It
concepts.body: Where a model is trained decides who owns which control. On Compute Engine or GKE, Google secures the infrastructure and hypervisor, while the customer owns the guest OS, images, patching, firewall rules, external IP exposure, the VM's service account and the training code. With managed custom training on the platform, Google runs and patches the training VMs, and the customer concentrates on identity, network placement, keys and data access. The default identity matters. Training containers run as the project's Custom Code Service Agent, a project-wide identity, so two teams sharing a project share whatever it can reach. Attach a user-managed service account to each CustomJob, HyperparameterTuningJob, TrainingPipeline or deployed model to scope permissions per team. A custom-trained model's prediction container runs as a platform-managed service account whose default access is limited to the model artifacts, so a model that must read a bucket in another project needs your service account attached at deployment. Workbench instances support your own VPC, CMEK and Confidential Computing chosen at creation.

concepts.heading: Perimeters, Private Paths and Keys
concepts.body: Platform APIs are reachable from the internet by default and rely on IAM. Private Service Connect for Google APIs and Private Google Access add private routes from your networks, but they do not remove the public path, so stolen valid credentials still work from outside. Add the platform API as a restricted service in a VPC Service Controls perimeter: public access is blocked unless the caller is allowed by an access level or ingress rule, and training data, models you created and similar artifacts cannot leave. The recommended private route uses the restricted VIP. Side effects follow. Pipelines run in a Google-managed producer project connected by peering; enabling VPC Service Controls for peerings with the restricted VIP removes the default route to the internet, so components that install packages at run time fail and should be prebuilt with dependencies. CMEK covers disks and temporary data on training VMs, dataset contents and model files, but not operation metadata such as job names, not in-memory data on endpoints, and batch prediction output follows the destination's encryption. CMEK is not an exfiltration control.

concepts.heading: Model Armor and Agent Blast Radius
concepts.body: Model Armor screens prompts and model responses for prompt injection and jailbreaks, harmful content, malicious URLs and sensitive data using Sensitive Data Protection. Gemini's configurable safety filters block harmful output by category but do not detect injection, redact account numbers or check URLs, so they are not a substitute. Templates hold filters and confidence thresholds. The documentation advises separate templates for input and output, since inputs focus on malicious prompts and uploaded sensitive data while outputs focus on leakage, harmful content and malicious URLs. The Low and above threshold flags even slight indications and causes many false positives, suited to high-stakes categories such as prompt injection; for general content start with High or Medium and above and test on representative prompts. Floor settings at organization, folder or project level set minimum requirements that templates must conform to, while teams may be stricter. An agent's tool calls run with an identity, so the blast radius of a successful injection equals that identity's permissions: give each agent a dedicated least-privilege identity.

examPoints: A question that demands zero data retention for a Gemini assistant points to disabling optional storage such as the Interactions API store setting and request-response logging, not to CMEK or to the training restriction alone.

A question where stolen credentials could pull training data from outside the company network, even with Private Service Connect in place, points to making the Agent Platform API a restricted service in a VPC Service Controls perimeter.

A question about a central minimum of prompt screening that teams may tighten points to Model Armor floor settings, and one about limiting what an injected agent can do points to a dedicated least-privilege agent identity.

quiz.q: Two teams share one project for custom training. Team A's jobs can read a bucket that only team B should reach, because jobs run with the project's default training identity. What is the best fix?
choices: Attach a user-managed service account to each team's jobs, with roles scoped to that team's data
Add a deny policy on the bucket's folder for team A and leave the shared default identity unchanged
Enable CMEK on the training jobs so that team A's reads of the bucket are encrypted differently
Move both teams into one perimeter so that perimeter rules separate their identities from each other
quiz.explain: The default Custom Code Service Agent is project-wide, so per-team service accounts attached to the jobs scope access properly. A deny on one path is brittle and leaves broad rights, CMEK does not partition identities, and a perimeter does not separate two teams inside it.

quiz.q: A bank's chatbot needs detection of prompt injection, redaction of account numbers in responses and flagging of malicious URLs. A developer proposes Gemini's configurable safety filters alone. What is the better answer?
choices: Keep the safety filters and add a Cloud Armor policy in front of the model's API endpoint
Use Model Armor with separate input and output templates and Sensitive Data Protection screening
Raise every safety filter threshold to the strictest value, which also covers injection and links
Add a system instruction that tells the model never to follow injected text or print any numbers
quiz.explain: Model Armor screens prompts and responses for injection, malicious URLs and sensitive data, and can redact or block. Safety filters cover harm categories only, Cloud Armor protects load-balanced apps rather than model calls, and instructions are not a security boundary.

days.recap: Training restriction is not zero retention, per-team identities and a VPC Service Controls perimeter shrink AI blast radius, and Model Armor plus least-privilege agent identities handle prompt-level threats.

days.title: Supply Chain Security: Image Scanning, Attestation and Admission Control, Trusted Sources and VM Patching

concepts.heading: Scanning Before Publication and Keeping Results Fresh
concepts.body: Artifact Analysis scans container images in two ways, and the stem's timing words choose between them. Automatic scanning runs when an image is pushed to Artifact Registry and then keeps the findings updated as new vulnerability data arrives, so it is detective: the image is already in the registry when the scan runs. On-Demand Scanning is started by a command, can scan an image stored locally without pushing it, and its results are available for up to 48 hours and are not updated afterward. To stop a vulnerable image from being published, add a Cloud Build step that runs On-Demand Scanning on the freshly built image, reads the severities and fails on HIGH or CRITICAL, so the push step never runs. Continuous updating has a catch: it continues only for images pulled within the last 30 days. After that the results go stale, and metadata stale for more than 90 days is archived and available only through the API. An eight-month-old image that nobody pulls and shows no new finding has not been proven clean, so rebuild and redeploy long-lived images in CI/CD.

concepts.heading: Binary Authorization: Attestors, Policies and Separation of Duties
concepts.body: Binary Authorization decides at deploy time whether an image may run. An attestation is a record, signed with a private key, stating that a specific image digest completed a stage such as QA or security review. An attestor is the resource that holds the matching public key and verifies those signatures. A rule in the require-attestations mode may list several attestors, and the image then needs attestations verified by all of them, so one attestor per approving team gives a logical AND. A policy has one default rule plus optional specific rules, which on GKE can target clusters, namespaces and Kubernetes service accounts. Put the strict requirement in the default rule and relax only the development cluster with a specific rule, so a cluster added later starts protected. Each project has exactly one policy, in the project where the platform runs. To stop a compromised CI service account from approving its own builds, use a multi-project setup: the deployment project holds only the policy, an attestor project holds the attestors and their verification keys, and an attestation project holds the records.

concepts.heading: Rolling Out and Operating Binary Authorization
concepts.body: Each rule has an evaluation mode (what is checked) and an enforcement mode (what happens on failure). Dry Run: Audit Log Only lets non-conformant images deploy but records them in Cloud Audit Logs, so a team can find unsigned pipelines before it switches to Block and Audit Log. Break-glass is the emergency path: a label on the Pod specification requests it, and every use is written to Cloud Audit Logs for review or alerting. A strict default can block GKE's own system Pods, which exempt image paths and trust of Google-maintained system images prevent. On Cloud Run only the default rule is supported, and the organization policy constraint run.allowedBinaryAuthorizationPolicies, set to the value default, requires enforcement in every project below it. A promoted copy of the same digest in another registry can reuse the attestation, but a rebuilt image has a new digest and needs a new one. Deploy-time checks do not flag running Pods. Continuous validation does monitor them, but its check-based form is Preview in the current documentation, so exam answers do not rely on it.

concepts.heading: Trusted Sources, Dependency Confusion and VM Patching
concepts.body: Controls on where artifacts come from sit beside image signing. The compute.trustedImageProjects organization policy limits which projects' images principals may use to create disks, but it does not restrict custom images in the local project, image files in Cloud Storage, or creating image resources locally, so a developer who can create images can still use them. Close that gap with IAM on image creation and detection. For packages, an Artifact Registry virtual repository fronts several upstream repositories of one format; higher priority values take precedence, equal priorities can be served from either, and leaving gaps lets you insert upstreams later. Dependency confusion happens when a public package shares an internal name, so rank the internal repository above the remote one. For VMs, VM Manager patch deployments install updates through the package manager and offer three reboot options: Default lets the agent decide, Always reboots, and Never does not, which in some cases leaves patches not fully applied. A scanner that still flags an old kernel after a successful run points to a reboot that never happened. The maintenance window limits when patching starts, not what runs afterward.

examPoints: A question that must stop a vulnerable image before it is pushed points to an On-Demand Scanning step in Cloud Build that fails on blocked severities, not to automatic scanning, which runs after the push.

A question that requires both QA and security approval, or approvals that a compromised CI account cannot forge, points to one attestor per team in a require-attestations rule, with the policy, attestors and attestations split across projects.

A question where a patch job reports success but the scanner still flags the old kernel points to the reboot option, and one that rolls out a new admission policy safely points to Dry Run: Audit Log Only before blocking.

quiz.q: A regulated company needs a production GKE cluster to run only images that the QA team and the application security team have each approved. Each team must keep its own signing key so that neither can forge the other's approval. Which Binary Authorization design fits?
choices: A default rule that requires attestations from two attestors, one per team, each with its team's public key
A default rule that lists a single attestor whose public key is shared by both teams for every signing operation
A default rule set to allow all images, with each team asking developers to avoid unapproved images by convention
A specific rule per namespace that requires one attestor, rotated between the two teams each release cycle
quiz.explain: When several attestors are listed in one rule, the image needs attestations verified by all of them, which gives a logical AND while each team keeps its own private key. A shared key lets either team forge the other's approval, allow-all enforces nothing, and one rotating attestor does not require both approvals.

quiz.q: A monthly VM Manager patch deployment for Linux VMs reports success, yet the vulnerability scanner flags the old kernel a day later. The deployment uses the reboot option Never. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The maintenance window was too short, so the fix is a longer window that lets the patch job run beyond its end time
The scanner caches results for a month, so the fix is a tag change on the image to trigger a fresh scan
The kernel update needs a restart to take effect, so the fix is the Default or Always reboot option
The patch job does not cover kernels, so the fix is an organization policy that forces every VM to be replaced
quiz.explain: A new kernel typically takes effect only after a restart, and the Never option does not reboot, so patches can be left not fully applied. The maintenance window only limits when patching starts, retagging an image does not change a running VM, and an organization policy cannot replace VMs.

days.recap: Gate the build with On-Demand Scanning, require one attestor per approving team at deploy time with duties split across projects, roll out in dry run, and remember that patching, trusted sources and stale scans each leave their own gap.

days.title: Posture and Drift: Custom Organization Policies, Security Posture and Custom Detectors

concepts.heading: Preventing and Detecting: Custom Constraints and Custom Modules
concepts.body: Posture work separates stopping a bad state from finding one. An organization policy is preventative. A custom constraint is written in CEL for a resource type and a method such as create, and it allows or denies matching requests. Policy changes are usually not retroactive: if the policy restricts a state that a resource is already in, the resource is in violation but the service does not stop its behavior, to protect business continuity, and violations must be fixed manually. Suppose a new hardening setting is required on every GKE cluster and several existing clusters already violate it. A custom constraint stops new violations without disrupting the old clusters, and a detective control finds the old ones. Security Health Analytics custom modules are that detective control: they are defined in YAML with CEL expressions, target any resource that Security Command Center supports, and write findings to Security Command Center. Test an organization policy before enforcing it. Policy Simulator shows how it would affect resources, and dry-run mode logs violations without denying them. Custom module findings are not covered by attack path simulation, so they carry no attack exposure scores.

concepts.heading: The Security Posture Service and Drift
concepts.body: Security Command Center includes a security posture service to define, deploy and monitor a posture. A posture is one or more policy sets, and each holds policies that are preventative (organization policy constraints, including custom constraints) or detective (Security Health Analytics detectors, including custom modules). Predefined templates follow standards such as CIS, NIST SP 800-53, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS, or Google-recommended settings. Essentials templates can be deployed without changes, while extended templates must be customized to match the environment first. A posture is deployed at an organization, folder or project, and only one posture can be deployed to each resource. Postures are inherited, and where a lower-level posture defines a policy differently, the lower-level definition is used below it, so the usual advice is a broad organization posture with stricter ones on production folders. After deployment, drift, an unauthorized change from the posture, is reported as Security Command Center findings that can be filtered and exported. The documentation says the service needs a paid Security Command Center tier activated at the organization level.

concepts.heading: Custom Detection Beyond the Predefined Detector
concepts.body: Predefined detectors are fixed, which is why a custom module exists. The predefined PUBLIC_SQL_INSTANCE detector flags a Cloud SQL instance whose authorized networks include 0.0.0.0/0. The documentation's example of a custom module matches address prefixes with wildcards, ignores instances in the MAINTENANCE state, or triggers only for specific regions. That is the answer when a stem needs a rule the predefined detector cannot express, and building a scheduled script that polls the API is the answer to avoid. Security Health Analytics checks the configuration of resources, so ask whether the signal is the state of a resource. Its detectors map to benchmark controls such as CIS, NIST, PCI-DSS and HIPAA. Event Threat Detection reads Cloud Logging and Google Workspace logs for events, and Virtual Machine Threat Detection scans VM instances for potentially malicious applications such as cryptocurrency mining software, so neither replaces a configuration check. Pairing a preventative constraint with a detective module for the same risk covers both new and existing resources.

concepts.heading: Guardrails with Gaps: Locations and Service Restriction
concepts.body: Two organization policy constraints are common guardrails, and each has documented limits. The resource locations constraint limits where new resources of supported services can be created. Resources created before the constraint continue to exist, global resources such as Compute Engine global addresses and resources with no location choice are not affected, some services are not enforced on sub-resource creation (Cloud Storage is one example), and a policy containing it is not a data storage commitment. Pair it with an inventory of existing resources and, for regulated scope, Assured Workloads monitoring. The Restrict Resource Service Usage constraint controls runtime access to all in-scope resources and applies to all access to all resources in scope, with eventual consistency, so a mistake is costly. It works in one of two mutually exclusive modes, a denylist or an allowlist, and it excludes essential dependencies such as IAM, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring. Use tags to scope enforcement conditionally, start with a pilot set of resources and widen after observing the impact. A Resource Manager tag in a conditional organization policy rule scopes a constraint inside a folder.

examPoints: A question that must block new violations without disrupting existing clusters points to a custom constraint in an organization policy, paired with a Security Health Analytics custom module to find the old violations.

A question that wants one set of preventative and detective controls deployed, inherited and monitored for drift points to the security posture service in Security Command Center, with extended templates customized before use.
A question where an auditor finds a global resource or an old resource despite an enforced locations policy points to the constraint's documented limits, not to a failure of the policy.

quiz.q: A security team adopts a requirement that every new GKE cluster must have a specific hardening setting, while several existing clusters already violate it. The team wants to stop new violations without disrupting the existing clusters and still see the old violations. Which combination fits?
choices: A custom constraint that denies noncompliant cluster creation, plus a Security Health Analytics custom module
A weekly export of cluster configurations to a spreadsheet, plus an email that asks cluster owners to fix their settings
A custom constraint alone, because the policy retroactively reports every existing noncompliant cluster as a finding
A deny policy in IAM that removes the cluster admin role from every engineer until each cluster is fixed
quiz.explain: A custom constraint prevents new violations and does not stop the behavior of existing resources, because policy changes are generally not retroactive. A Security Health Analytics custom module is the detective control that writes findings for resources that already violate the rule. A manual export, a constraint on its own, or an IAM deny would leave a gap or cause disruption.

quiz.q: A platform team wants to deploy a broad set of organization policy constraints and Security Health Analytics detectors to the whole organization and stricter ones to the production folder, and be told when someone changes a setting. Which service fits?
choices: Policy Simulator, which previews a change but does not deploy policies or report later changes
The security posture service, which deploys inherited postures and reports drift as findings
Cloud Asset Inventory, which lists resources but does not evaluate or enforce any posture
Access Approval, which asks an approver to consent before Google staff may touch resources
quiz.explain: The security posture service defines postures made of preventative and detective policies, deploys them at the organization, folder or project level with inheritance, and reports unauthorized changes as drift findings. The other services preview, list or gate different things.

days.recap: Prevent with custom constraints, detect with Security Health Analytics custom modules, deploy and monitor both as a posture, and remember that policy is not retroactive and locations and service restriction have documented gaps.

days.title: Network Telemetry: Firewall Logs, VPC Flow Logs, Packet Mirroring, Cloud IDS and Observability Analytics

concepts.heading: Rule Logs Versus Flow Logs: Which Question Each Answers
concepts.body: Firewall policy rules logging and VPC Flow Logs are different telemetry for different questions. Rules logging writes a record when a connection is established and answers which rule allowed or denied it. A connection stays active while packets are exchanged at least once every 10 minutes, so a continuous stream produces one entry for its whole life, and only TCP and UDP connections are recorded. If logging is turned on for a rule that matches an already active connection, no new entry is generated until the connection has been idle for at least 10 minutes and a new packet is sent. VPC Flow Logs sample packets and aggregate them by 5-tuple over an aggregation interval, so a long-lived connection produces entries throughout, and they describe volume and timing for monitoring and forensics. Suppose responders suspect a VM holds one TCP connection to an external server for hours and moves data. Rules logging shows the single allow decision, while flow logs show the ongoing transfer. Neither records payload. Turn logging on before the activity you want to investigate.

concepts.heading: Flow Log Scope and the Short-Connection Blind Spot
concepts.body: Flow logs can be enabled at the organization, VPC network, subnet, VLAN attachment and Cloud VPN tunnel scopes, and at project level for specific networks, subnets, attachments or tunnels. An organization-level configuration enables flow logs for all subnets, VLAN attachments and Cloud VPN tunnels in all VPC networks in the organization, so resources created later are included, which fits a company that keeps creating projects. Logs go to Cloud Logging in the project of the VPC network that reported the flow and are stored for 30 days by default; keep them longer with a custom retention period or by exporting them. Sampling has a cost. The primary sampling rate is dynamic and cannot be adjusted, and an optional secondary rate applies after aggregation, so short-lived or low-volume TCP connections can be missed, which is exactly what a port scan produces. The optional TCP connection logging setting captures all outbound TCP connection attempts (the initial SYN) and all acknowledged inbound connections (the SYN-ACK reply) for VM instances and serverless endpoints, and it can be set for a subnet, a VPC network or an organization.

concepts.heading: Packet Mirroring and Cloud IDS
concepts.body: When flow metadata is not enough, Packet Mirroring clones the traffic of selected instances, including payloads and headers, and forwards it for examination. Sources are Compute Engine instances chosen by subnet, network tags or instance names, and the collector is an instance group behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer whose forwarding rule is enabled for mirroring. Filters limit the extra bandwidth that mirroring consumes on the VMs. All sources in one policy must be in the same project, VPC network and region, and the collector must be in that region too, so mirroring two regions needs two policies. Cloud IDS builds on mirrored traffic: an endpoint attached to a mirroring policy detects exploit attempts and spyware. Tune it with a minimum alert severity for the whole set, or with threat exceptions that disable specific threat IDs, limited to 99 per endpoint; one confirmed false positive is a threat exception, not a higher severity. Cloud NGFW Layer 7 inspection and a Cloud IDS endpoint must not apply to the same traffic, because the inspection policy takes priority and the traffic is not mirrored.

concepts.heading: Analyzing Network Logs: Observability Analytics and Field Access
concepts.body: Logs Explorer is for troubleshooting and exploration and does not support aggregate operations such as counting entries. Observability Analytics, previously called Log Analytics, runs SQL over log buckets that have been upgraded to use analytics, with grouping, aggregation, charting and joins of log and trace data. For the top talkers by hour across several months of flow logs, upgrade the bucket and query it, and create a linked BigQuery dataset when BigQuery needs to query the same data without ingesting a second copy. The bucket must be created at project level and unlocked, unless it is the _Required bucket, and logs written before the upgrade need a backfill that can take several days. Field-level access controls change the picture. A bucket can hide fields such as source IP addresses from some principals, but you cannot use the Observability Analytics page to query log views when the bucket has field-level access controls, and BigQuery does not honor them, so anyone who can query the linked dataset can read all fields. Grant the dataset only to people entitled to every field, or give restricted analysts another path such as Logs Explorer.

examPoints: A question where responders need to follow a long-lived connection for hours points to VPC Flow Logs, because firewall rules logging records a connection once when it is established.

A question about complete packet payloads for a third-party detection appliance points to Packet Mirroring with a collector behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, one policy per region.

A question about top talkers by hour with SQL and no second copy of the logs points to a log bucket upgraded to Observability Analytics, with a linked BigQuery dataset only for people entitled to every field.

quiz.q: Incident responders suspect a compromised VM keeps one long-lived TCP connection open to an external server and transfers data over hours. Cloud NGFW firewall policy rules logging shows only one allow entry at the start. Which telemetry shows the ongoing transfer?
choices: Packet Mirroring to an IDS collector, because it is the only telemetry that records sampled flow volumes over time
A second logging toggle on the same rule, because it forces new entries for each packet in an active connection
Cloud Audit Logs Admin Activity entries, because they list each data transfer made by a running virtual machine
VPC Flow Logs, because they aggregate sampled packets per 5-tuple so a long connection yields entries throughout
quiz.explain: Rules logging records a connection when it is established, once for as long as packets keep moving, while flow logs aggregate sampled packets over each interval and so describe an ongoing flow. Mirroring captures full packets rather than sampled flow records, and audit logs record administrative actions, not network volume.

quiz.q: A forensics team created one Packet Mirroring policy to mirror web VMs in two regions of the same VPC network to a single collector group in one region. The policy is rejected. What is the correct design?
choices: Create one policy per region, each with its own collector group behind an internal passthrough load balancer
Create one policy that selects sources by network tag instead of by subnet, which removes the regional requirement
Move the collector to a different project so it can receive mirrored traffic from instances in both regions
Replace the policy with a VPC Flow Logs configuration, because only that feature can capture packet payloads
quiz.explain: All mirrored sources of a policy must be in the same project, VPC network and region, and the collector must be in that region, so two regions need two policies and two collectors. The selection method does not remove the regional limit, and flow logs do not capture payloads.

days.recap: Use rules logging to prove which rule decided, flow logs (with TCP connection logging for short probes) to follow traffic, Packet Mirroring and Cloud IDS for payload and threats, and Observability Analytics for SQL, minding field-level access.

days.title: Audit Logs and Detection: Cloud Audit Logs, Log Router Sinks, Evidence Protection and Security Command Center

concepts.heading: Audit Log Types and Who Can Read Them
concepts.body: Cloud Audit Logs has four types. Admin Activity records configuration and metadata changes and is always on. System Event is written by Google Cloud systems for changes not driven by a user, and it cannot be disabled. Policy Denied is written when a service denies access because of a security policy violation, and it is on by default; you may keep it out of storage with exclusion filters but cannot disable generation. Data Access records reads and writes of data and metadata and, except for BigQuery, is disabled by default. Its configuration is part of an IAM policy that lists per service the log types ADMIN_READ, DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE to record. A noisy nightly job running as one service account is handled with an exempted principal under that log type, a deliberate audit gap to document, not by weakening the configuration for everybody. Organization, folder and project configurations combine as a union, so a lower level can add but cannot switch off what a higher level enabled. Reading them is separate: Logs Viewer sees the _Required and _Default buckets except Data Access logs, and Private Logs Viewer adds those.

concepts.heading: Routing Logs: Sinks, Aggregated Sinks and Destinations
concepts.body: In the Log Router every sink in a resource evaluates an entry independently, and a sink sends it on when it matches the inclusion filter and none of the sink's own exclusion filters. An exclusion on the _Default sink therefore changes what that bucket stores but not what other sinks receive, and it does not stop the entry from being generated. Aggregated sinks at a folder or organization cover every present and future child. A non-intercepting aggregated sink copies entries and leaves child sinks alone, which suits a security copy. An intercepting one stops matching entries from reaching sinks in child resources, apart from the _Required sink, so application logs disappear from project _Default buckets while Admin Activity entries still appear. Choose the destination by purpose. Pub/Sub delivers continuously to an external SIEM, and an inclusion filter on audit logs keeps per-gigabyte licence cost down. Cloud Storage suits cheap seven-year retention that is read rarely, BigQuery suits SQL analysis, and log buckets keep entries searchable in Cloud Logging. The sink's writer identity needs a role on the destination, such as roles/storage.objectCreator on a bucket.

concepts.heading: Protecting Log Evidence
concepts.body: Logs are evidence about the people who operate workloads, so keep them away from those people. Copy audit logs with an aggregated sink at the organization or folder into a dedicated project that the security team controls. Retention on a log bucket ranges from 1 to 3650 days for a custom bucket and defaults to 30 days. Locking a bucket makes its retention period impossible to shorten and the bucket impossible to delete until every entry has fulfilled the retention. The lock is permanent, so choose the value carefully, and pair it with a project lien. A sink into a Cloud Storage bucket inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter needs an ingress rule for the sink's identity; for an aggregated sink the documented identity type is ANY_IDENTITY, and the fix is a narrow rule for storage.googleapis.com and the destination project. Log views, each with its own IAM policy, let one central bucket serve many teams; a bucket can have up to 30 views. Default resource settings can set a Cloud KMS key for new buckets in an organization or folder, and a bucket's location must match the key's location.

concepts.heading: Detection and Response with Security Command Center
concepts.body: Match the signal to the detector. Security Health Analytics checks resource configuration, such as a public bucket. Event Threat Detection reads Cloud Logging and Google Workspace logs for events, and each rule lists the log sources it needs: a rule built on IAM Data Access DATA_READ logs cannot detect those events until those logs are enabled. Virtual Machine Threat Detection finds potentially malicious applications such as cryptominers, and Container Threat Detection finds runtime attacks. The documentation describes Event Threat Detection as a Security Command Center Premium tier service. Muting hides acceptable findings while scanners keep running; dynamic mute rules apply to existing and new findings and can expire, a static rule takes precedence when both match, and Security Command Center recommends dynamic rules only. New findings can go to Pub/Sub in near real time with a filter such as state ACTIVE. For a break-glass account, route audit logs to a central project and use a log-based alert on its principal. In an incident, disable the key or account, preserve logs and disks, investigate, then recover; deleting the project erases evidence.

examPoints: A question where an auditor sees Admin Activity entries but no data reads points to Data Access logs being off or readable only with Private Logs Viewer, not to a missing sink.

A question that needs a tamper-resistant copy of audit logs outside workload administrators' control points to an organization aggregated sink into a dedicated project with a locked bucket and a project lien.
A question about a threat rule that never fires points to the log types the rule requires, such as IAM Data Access logs, being disabled.

quiz.q: A platform team creates an intercepting aggregated sink at the organization level that matches all entries from projects under one folder. Afterward, application logs vanish from the _Default buckets of those projects, while Admin Activity entries still appear. What explains this?
choices: An intercepting sink blocks matching entries from child sinks, except _Required, which still holds Admin Activity
Admin Activity logs are copied twice by every aggregated sink, so the application logs were removed to save space
The intercepting sink deleted entries from the _Default bucket because exclusion filters apply to existing entries
Data Access logs were disabled for the folder, and application logs are a subtype of Data Access logs
quiz.explain: An intercepting aggregated sink stops matching entries from reaching sinks in child resources, with the exception of the _Required sink, which always receives its entries. Application logs normally reach _Default through a child sink, so they stop arriving there. Exclusions do not delete stored entries, and application logs are not Data Access logs.

quiz.q: A SIEM is licensed per ingested gigabyte, and the security team needs near-real-time audit events from every project, including future ones, while investigators keep full logs. Which design fits?
choices: An organization sink to Cloud Storage with no filter, because batch files arrive faster than any streaming path
Per-project sinks to Pub/Sub that each team creates by hand, with no filter, so the SIEM sees every entry
An exclusion filter on the _Default sink for audit logs, so the SIEM reads the smaller bucket
An organization aggregated sink to Pub/Sub with an audit-log inclusion filter, and full copies kept in buckets
quiz.explain: An aggregated sink covers projects created later, Pub/Sub delivers continuously for near-real-time ingestion, and an inclusion filter keeps the licensed volume narrow. Full copies stay in buckets for investigation. Batch files add delay, manual per-project sinks miss new projects, and an exclusion on one sink does not change what other sinks receive.

days.recap: Know which audit logs are always on, route them with non-intercepting aggregated sinks to a locked central copy, send a filtered stream to the SIEM, and match each Security Command Center detector to the signal it actually reads.

days.title: Compliance Foundations: Shared Responsibility, Scoping, Mapping Controls and Assured Workloads

concepts.heading: Shared Responsibility Moves with the Service Model
concepts.body: Under the shared responsibility model, Google is always responsible for the underlying network and infrastructure, and customers always remain responsible for their access policies and data. In between, responsibility moves with the service type. For IaaS such as Compute Engine, the customer handles most controls, including guest OS patching and network configuration. For PaaS such as GKE and BigQuery, Google handles more, while the customer still owns application-level controls, IAM and data security. A function on Cloud Run functions is an example of serverless shifting infrastructure but not code: Google is responsible for the function platform, and the customer for application logic, third-party packages in the deployment artifact, secrets handling and invoker permissions. So when a critical vulnerability is announced in a bundled open-source library, patching it is the customer's job, and dependency scanning in the build pipeline helps. A leaked service account key is also on the customer side, because credentials are part of access policy, so the customer owns detection and response in its resources and prevention through disabled key creation and short-lived credentials.

concepts.heading: Scoping and Mapping Requirements to Controls
concepts.body: Scoping starts from the data. Identify where regulated data is stored, processed or transmitted, then trace connectivity and access paths such as Shared VPC, peering and VPN, IAM trust, service accounts and shared secrets or keys, and include components that can affect the security of those systems. Put the in-scope projects in a dedicated folder with organization policies, firewall segmentation and logging, so a smaller environment needs controls and evidence. As a common scoping practice, keep regulated and non-regulated work in separate projects, because everything that shares a project with regulated data is hard to argue out of scope. For a mixed estate with on-premises systems, Compute Engine, GKE and BigQuery, build a matrix with service, data flow, regulation control, owner (Google or customer) and evidence. On-premises systems are entirely the customer's, and the customer must consider how controls for different services interact, for example data in transit between them. A requirement for physical security of data centers is an inherited control: answer it with Google's reports and certifications from the Compliance resource center, and still evidence your own IAM, network rules, encryption choices, logging and VM patching.

concepts.heading: Assured Workloads Control Packages
concepts.body: Assured Workloads groups control packages by the assurance they give. Regional data boundaries enforce data residency, with optional personnel controls in the "and Support" variants. Regulatory data boundaries deploy certified controls tailored to a specific regulation. Sovereign Controls by Partners are operated by a partner who manages encryption keys, access justification and audits. Start from who must operate the control: a Swiss bank that wants a local partner to manage keys and judge access justifications needs the partner-operated family, since residency alone does not provide it. A plain data boundary such as Canada Data Boundary restricts where resources are stored and used, not which Google support personnel handle a case. The "and Support" variants are listed in the Premium pricing tier, plain data boundaries in the Free tier, and personnel controls rely on Assured Support for Assured Workloads, which is available with Enhanced Support or Premium Support. Key rules differ by package. CJIS, ITAR and IL5 mandate customer-managed encryption keys and a separate key management project. Other packages such as IL4 allow Google-managed keys, with CMEK, Cloud EKM and key import optional.

concepts.heading: Folders, Existing Projects and Violation Monitoring
concepts.body: Creating an Assured Workloads folder selects an organization, a location in the hierarchy and a control package. The organization cannot be changed later. If Access Transparency is not enabled on the organization, it is enabled automatically at folder creation, and projects created or moved into the folder are configured to use it. The folder applies an organization policy that restricts resource usage to the package's supported products and allowed locations. For a project that already exists, analyze it against the package, make the required changes and then move it into the folder, because moving does not repair a noncompliant resource. Monitoring is enabled automatically at folder creation and compares organization policy settings under the folder with the package; resource violation monitoring can be enabled on the folder. A violation is Unresolved, Resolved (remediated) or Exception (accepted with a business justification). By default the Legal category of Essential Contacts is emailed, so add the security team to that category to receive the same notices. Viewing violations needs a read role such as Assured Workloads Reader; adding an exception needs violations.update, included in the Assured Workloads Administrator and Editor roles.
